\hypertarget{heat-flows-from-hot-to-cold-as-a-theorem-of-dxux2084dt-ic-thermodynamics-paper-24-theorem-9b-of-24}{%
\paragraph{6.2.9 Heat flows from hot to cold as a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic
(thermodynamics paper {[}24{]}, Theorem 9b of
{[}24{]})}\label{heat-flows-from-hot-to-cold-as-a-theorem-of-dxux2084dt-ic-thermodynamics-paper-24-theorem-9b-of-24}}

\textbf{Theorem (Heat-flow directionality).} Let \(A\) and \(B\) be two
Compton-coupled massive-particle ensembles, each at internal thermal
equilibrium under the Compton-coupled Brownian dynamics of Theorems 4-6
of {[}24{]}, with kinetic temperatures \(T_A > T_B\) defined by
\(\tfrac{3}{2}\kB T = \langle E_{\rm kin}\rangle\) on each ensemble.
Place \(A\) and \(B\) in thermal contact across a permeable interface
\(\Sigma\) across which particles cross via Compton-coupled Brownian
transport. The net rate of kinetic-energy transfer across \(\Sigma\) is
from \(A\) (hot) to \(B\) (cold), strict: \(\dot Q_{A \to B} > 0\). The
reverse direction would violate the strict Second Law of Theorem 9 of
{[}24{]}, hence violate the \(+ic\) orientation of \(dx_4/dt = ic\).
Heat flow from hot to cold is therefore a theorem of \(dx_4/dt = ic\).

\emph{Proof.} The proof proceeds in five steps: a kinetic-theory
definition of temperature (Step 1); a Compton-coupling-internal
derivation that collision rate scales linearly with particle speed (Step
2); a derivation that the equilibrium velocity distribution under
Compton-coupled Brownian dynamics is Maxwell-Boltzmann (Step 3); the
speed-asymmetry calculation of the interfacial energy flux (Step 4); and
the closure that traces the strict positivity to the \(+ic\) orientation
via Theorem 9 of {[}24{]} (Step 5).

\textbf{Step 1 (Kinetic-theory definition of temperature from
Compton-coupled Brownian dynamics).} Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a
Compton-coupled massive-particle ensemble of \(N\) particles of mass
\(m\) undergoing Brownian motion in the sense of Theorem 6 of {[}24{]},
with the per-particle Wiener-process density at large times approaching
the equilibrium Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution (Step 3 below).
The kinetic temperature of \(\mathcal{E}\) is the parameter \(T\) in the
equipartition identity

\[\tfrac{3}{2}\kB T \;=\; \langle E_{\rm kin}\rangle \;=\; \langle \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2\rangle, \tag{9b.1}\]

where \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) denotes the ensemble average over the
\(N\) particles. The factor \(\tfrac{3}{2}\) is the standard
equipartition factor for three translational degrees of freedom; the
identity (9b.1) is the \emph{definition} of \(T\) in the kinetic-theory
sense. The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at \(T\) has root-mean-square
speed \(v_{\rm rms} = \sqrt{3\kB T/m}\) and mean speed
\(\bar v = \sqrt{8\kB T/(\pi m)}\). Higher \(T\) corresponds to higher
\(\bar v\) in a strict monotone relationship.

\textbf{Step 2 (Collision rate scales linearly with particle speed:
Compton-coupling-internal derivation).} Consider a single
Compton-coupled particle of mass \(m\) moving with instantaneous speed
\(v\) through a medium of fixed scatterer number density \(n_s\) and
effective scattering cross-section \(\sigma_s\). We derive the collision
rate \(\nu(v)\) as a content of the Compton-coupling of Theorem 4 of
{[}24{]}.

By Theorem 4 of {[}24{]}, the particle's worldline advances along
\(x_4\) at the rate \(ic\) {[}\(dx_4/dt = ic\) in coordinate time, the
proper-time reading coinciding on the rest worldline where
\(d\tau = dt\), Lemma 4.7 of {[}29{]}{]}, with the rest-frame phase
accumulating at the Compton frequency \(\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar\). The
spatial projection of this \(x_4\)-advance onto the spatial three-slice
(Theorem 5 of {[}24{]}) produces, in any inertial frame in which the
particle has spatial speed \(v\), a spatial trajectory that traverses
arc length \(v\,dt\) in coordinate time \(dt\).

The trajectory swept by the particle in time \(dt\) is, on the spatial
three-slice, a tube of length \(v\,dt\) and cross-section \(\sigma_s\)
(the effective scattering cross-section). The volume of this tube is
\(\sigma_s\, v\, dt\). The number of scatterers within this swept volume
-- equivalently, the number of collision events the particle undergoes
in time \(dt\) -- is

\[dN_{\rm coll}(v) \;=\; n_s\, \sigma_s\, v\, dt, \tag{9b.2}\]

so the collision rate per particle is

\[\nu(v) \;=\; \frac{dN_{\rm coll}}{dt} \;=\; n_s\, \sigma_s\, v. \tag{9b.3}\]

The collision rate is linear in \(v\). This is a direct content of
Theorem 4 of {[}24{]} plus the geometric fact that spatial arc length
per unit coordinate time equals \(v\) for a particle of spatial speed
\(v\); no auxiliary kinetic-theory postulate is invoked. Faster
Compton-coupled particles sweep more spatial volume per unit time and
undergo collisions at a proportionally higher rate.

\textbf{Step 3 (Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution as equilibrium
of Compton-coupled Brownian dynamics).} By Theorem 6 of {[}24{]}, the
spatial density \(\rho(\mathbf{r}, t)\) of a Compton-coupled
massive-particle ensemble satisfies the Wiener-process diffusion
equation \(\partial_t \rho = D \nabla^2 \rho\). The equilibrium
distribution in \emph{velocity space} under the Compton-coupled Langevin
dynamics of Theorem 14 of {[}24{]} -- that is, under the Langevin
equation
\(m \dot{\mathbf{v}} = -m\gamma \mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\) with
thermal noise satisfying
\(\langle \xi_i(t)\xi_j(t')\rangle = 2 D_p \delta_{ij}\delta(t-t')\) --
is obtained from the velocity-space Fokker-Planck equation

\[\frac{\partial f(\mathbf{v},t)}{\partial t} \;=\; \gamma \nabla_{\mathbf v}\cdot(\mathbf{v} f) + \frac{D_p}{m^2} \nabla_{\mathbf v}^2 f. \tag{9b.4}\]

Stationarity \(\partial_t f = 0\) together with the boundary condition
\(f \to 0\) as \(|\mathbf{v}| \to \infty\) has unique solution

\[f_{\rm eq}(\mathbf{v}) \;=\; \left(\frac{m}{2\pi \kB T}\right)^{3/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{m|\mathbf{v}|^2}{2\kB T}\right), \qquad \kB T \;=\; \frac{D_p}{m\gamma}, \tag{9b.5}\]

where the second identification is the Einstein fluctuation-dissipation
relation. This is the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at kinetic
temperature \(T\) defined by (9b.1). Equation (9b.5) is the equilibrium
velocity-space density forced by the Compton-coupled Langevin dynamics;
under (9b.5), the mean kinetic energy satisfies
\(\langle \tfrac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}\kB T\) by
direct Gaussian integration, recovering (9b.1) and confirming the
consistency of the kinetic-temperature definition. The Maxwell-Boltzmann
distribution is the unique stationary state of Compton-coupled Brownian
motion; it is not separately postulated.

The relevant consequence: the mean particle speed in an ensemble at
temperature \(T\) is

\[\bar v(T) \;=\; \int_0^\infty v\, f_{\rm eq}(\mathbf{v})\, 4\pi v^2\, dv \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{8\kB T}{\pi m}}. \tag{9b.6}\]

The mean speed grows as \(\sqrt T\). Hotter ensembles have faster mean
particle speeds in a strict monotone relationship.

\textbf{Step 4 (Speed-asymmetry interfacial flux: hotter side delivers
more particle crossings per unit time per unit area, hence more energy
crossings).} Consider the interface \(\Sigma\) between ensembles \(A\)
(temperature \(T_A\), particle number density \(n_A\)) and \(B\)
(temperature \(T_B < T_A\), particle number density \(n_B\)) with
\(\Sigma\) permeable to particle crossing. Assume for clarity that
\(n_A = n_B = n\); the unequal-density case is a straightforward
extension treated at the end of the step.

By the spatial-projection isotropy of Theorem 5 of {[}24{]}, the
velocity directions of particles arriving at \(\Sigma\) from either side
are uniformly distributed on the unit two-sphere. The flux of particles
across \(\Sigma\) from side \(A\) to side \(B\) -- defined as the number
of particles per unit area per unit time crossing \(\Sigma\) in the
\(A\to B\) direction -- is obtained by integrating the velocity-space
density \(f_{\rm eq}\) at temperature \(T_A\) over the half-space of
velocities pointing from \(A\) to \(B\), weighted by the normal
component of velocity:

\[\Phi_{A\to B}^{(\rm particles)} \;=\; n \int_{v_\perp > 0} v_\perp\, f_{\rm eq}(\mathbf{v}; T_A)\, d^3 v \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4} n \bar v(T_A), \tag{9b.7}\]

where \(v_\perp\) is the velocity component normal to \(\Sigma\)
pointing from \(A\) to \(B\), the integral is taken over the hemisphere
\(v_\perp > 0\), and the factor \(\tfrac{1}{4}\) is the standard
kinetic-theory factor obtained by direct evaluation (mean projection of
an isotropic velocity onto an axis, restricted to one hemisphere,
multiplied by the half-space probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)). The same
calculation applied to side \(B\) gives the reverse particle flux

\[\Phi_{B\to A}^{(\rm particles)} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4} n \bar v(T_B). \tag{9b.8}\]

By (9b.6) and \(T_A > T_B\), \(\bar v(T_A) > \bar v(T_B)\), so

\[\Phi_{A\to B}^{(\rm particles)} \;>\; \Phi_{B\to A}^{(\rm particles)} \;>\; 0. \tag{9b.9}\]

More particles cross from hot to cold per unit time per unit area than
from cold to hot. This is the \textbf{speed asymmetry} the question
identifies: at equal number density, hotter particles move faster, sweep
more spatial volume per unit time (Step 2), and consequently cross any
fixed interface at higher frequency.

Each particle crossing \(\Sigma\) carries kinetic energy. The energy
flux from \(A\) to \(B\) is obtained by replacing the integrand
\(v_\perp\) in (9b.7) with
\(v_\perp \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} m |\mathbf{v}|^2\), integrating over the
\(v_\perp > 0\) hemisphere weighted by \(f_{\rm eq}(T_A)\). The standard
kinetic-theory evaluation gives

\[\Phi_{A\to B}^{(\rm energy)} \;=\; n \cdot \tfrac{1}{4} \bar v(T_A) \cdot \langle E_{\rm kin}\rangle_A^{(\rm crossing)} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4} n \bar v(T_A) \cdot 2 \kB T_A \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2} n \kB T_A \bar v(T_A), \tag{9b.10}\]

where \(\langle E_{\rm kin}\rangle_A^{(\rm crossing)} = 2\kB T_A\) is
the mean kinetic energy of \emph{crossing} particles (which exceeds the
bulk-ensemble mean kinetic energy \(\tfrac{3}{2}\kB T_A\) because the
crossing flux is preferentially weighted toward higher-\(v_\perp\)
particles via the \(v_\perp\) factor in the integrand). The reverse
energy flux is

\[\Phi_{B\to A}^{(\rm energy)} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2} n \kB T_B \bar v(T_B). \tag{9b.11}\]

The net energy flux from \(A\) to \(B\) is

\[\dot Q_{A\to B} \;=\; \Phi_{A\to B}^{(\rm energy)} - \Phi_{B\to A}^{(\rm energy)} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2} n \kB \bigl[ T_A \bar v(T_A) - T_B \bar v(T_B) \bigr]. \tag{9b.12}\]

Substituting \(\bar v(T) = \sqrt{8\kB T/(\pi m)}\) from (9b.6):

\[\dot Q_{A\to B} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2} n \kB \sqrt{\tfrac{8\kB}{\pi m}} \left( T_A^{3/2} - T_B^{3/2} \right). \tag{9b.13}\]

Since \(T_A > T_B > 0\), \(T_A^{3/2} > T_B^{3/2}\) strict, and therefore

\[\dot Q_{A\to B} \;>\; 0 \quad\text{strict}. \tag{9b.14}\]

Energy flows from \(A\) (hot) to \(B\) (cold), with the inequality
strict whenever \(T_A > T_B\). The unequal-density case \(n_A \neq n_B\)
replaces (9b.13) with
\(\tfrac{1}{2}\kB\sqrt{8\kB/(\pi m)}\,[n_A T_A^{3/2} - n_B T_B^{3/2}]\),
which is positive whenever the temperature gradient dominates the
density gradient (the standard heat-conduction regime); the pure
temperature-gradient case (9b.13) is the directionally clean result.

\textbf{Step 5 (Closure: the strict positivity in (9b.14) traces to the
\(+ic\) orientation via Theorem 9 of {[}24{]}).} The combined ensemble
\(A \cup B\) is itself a Compton-coupled massive-particle ensemble (the
union of two such), so by Theorem 9 of {[}24{]} the total kinetic-theory
entropy of the combined ensemble satisfies \(dS_{A\cup B}/dt > 0\)
strict. The contribution of the heat transfer (9b.13) to the entropy
budget is

\[\frac{dS_{A\cup B}}{dt}\bigg|_{\rm transfer} \;=\; -\frac{\dot Q_{A\to B}}{T_A} + \frac{\dot Q_{A\to B}}{T_B} \;=\; \dot Q_{A\to B}\left(\frac{1}{T_B} - \frac{1}{T_A}\right). \tag{9b.15}\]

Since \(T_A > T_B\), we have \(1/T_B > 1/T_A\), so
\((1/T_B - 1/T_A) > 0\) strict. Combined with (9b.14), the transfer
contributes

\[\frac{dS_{A\cup B}}{dt}\bigg|_{\rm transfer} \;>\; 0 \quad\text{strict}. \tag{9b.16}\]

The strict inequality in (9b.14) -- that energy flows from hot to cold
-- is precisely the inequality that makes (9b.16) positive rather than
negative, hence consistent with Theorem 9 of {[}24{]}'s
strict-positive-entropy-production. The hypothetical reverse direction
\(\dot Q_{A\to B} < 0\) (energy flowing from cold to hot at a permeable
interface, with no other change) would produce
\(dS_{A\cup B}/dt|_{\rm transfer} < 0\), violating Theorem 9 of
{[}24{]}. Since Theorem 9 of {[}24{]} traces directly to the \(+ic\)
orientation of \(dx_4/dt = ic\) (the strict positivity \(D > 0\) of the
diffusion coefficient in the Wiener equation is the spatial-projection
content of \(+ic\), not \(-ic\), expansion of the McGucken Sphere; see
Theorem 9 of {[}24{]} Steps A3, B4), the directionality of heat flow
traces to the \(+ic\) orientation in exactly the same way.

Equivalently: were \(dx_4/dt = -ic\) to hold, the Wiener-process
diffusion coefficient \(D\) would carry the reverse sign, the
equilibrium Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution (9b.5) would not be
normalizable as a forward-time stationary state, the mean speed
\(\bar v(T)\) would be ill-defined as a \(+t\)-asymptotic quantity, and
the interfacial flux calculation (9b.13) would invert. The \(+\) in
\(+ic\) is what fixes the direction of heat flow.

Combining Steps 1-5: heat flow from hot to cold is a theorem of
\(dx_4/dt = ic\) via the chain Compton coupling (T4) \(\to\)
spatial-projection isotropy (T5) \(\to\) Brownian motion (T6) \(\to\)
Maxwell-Boltzmann equilibrium velocity distribution (Step 3 above)
\(\to\) collision rate linear in speed (Step 2 above) \(\to\)
interfacial flux asymmetry (Step 4 above) \(\to\) strict
entropy-production closure (Step 5 above, via T9 and its \(+ic\) trace).
The Clausius statement of the Second Law -- no spontaneous process whose
sole effect is the transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter body -- is
the inequality (9b.14) read in the contrapositive direction, and it is a
theorem of \(dx_4/dt = ic\) in the same sense. ?

\emph{Diagnostic remark.} The mechanism is what Maxwell 1860 {[}222{]}
gave as the kinetic-theory explanation of heat conduction: hotter
particles move faster, sweep more spatial volume per unit time, and
consequently cross any fixed interface at a higher rate, delivering
kinetic energy preferentially in the down-temperature-gradient
direction. The McGucken framing identifies the source of every step in
Maxwell's argument: Compton coupling (Theorem 4 of {[}24{]}) supplies
the universal mass-energy oscillation that gives every particle the same
rate of \(x_4\)-phase accumulation; spatial-projection isotropy (Theorem
5 of {[}24{]}) supplies the SO(3)-symmetric velocity-direction
distribution; Brownian motion (Theorem 6 of {[}24{]}) supplies the
diffusive transport equation; the Maxwell-Boltzmann equilibrium (Step 3
of the present theorem) is the unique stationary state of
Compton-coupled Brownian dynamics; the collision-rate-linear-in-speed
(Step 2) is direct from the spatial arc length swept per unit coordinate
time. The Maxwell 1860 calculation closes through Theorem 9 of
{[}24{]}'s strict-positivity content, which carries the \(+ic\)
orientation of \(dx_4/dt = ic\). The physical fact ``hotter particles
move faster and hit more particles than slower ones'' is, in the
McGucken framing, the empirical surface of the deeper fact that the
Compton-coupled \(x_4\)-advance produces Maxwell-Boltzmann equilibrium
with strict monotone speed-temperature relationship.

\emph{Consequences for the Carnot, Kelvin, and Clausius statements.} The
Carnot cycle bound (Theorem proved in the Geometric-Channel Founders
section), the Kelvin-Planck statement of the Second Law (no process
whose sole result is the transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter
body), and the Clausius statement (no spontaneous heat flow from cold to
hot) are corollaries of the present Theorem 9b of {[}24{]}: each is the
statement that the inequality (9b.14) cannot be reversed, with the
irreversibility traced to the \(+ic\) orientation through Theorem 9 of
{[}24{]}. The hand-waved ``\(+ic\)-monotonic content forces heat from
hot to cold'' of the earlier Carnot Step 3 derivation is replaced by the
explicit chain of the present proof.

\hypertarget{the-mcgucken-measurement-theorem-quantum-measurement-is-the-wick-rotation-performed-physically-by-the-apparatus-thermodynamics-paper-24-theorem-25-of-24}{%
\paragraph{6.2.10 The McGucken Measurement Theorem --- quantum
measurement is the Wick rotation performed physically by the apparatus
(thermodynamics paper {[}24{]}, Theorem 25 of
{[}24{]})}\label{the-mcgucken-measurement-theorem-quantum-measurement-is-the-wick-rotation-performed-physically-by-the-apparatus-thermodynamics-paper-24-theorem-25-of-24}}

We now establish the deepest single application of the McGucken-Wick
rotation to laboratory physics: the act of quantum measurement is the
McGucken-Wick rotation \(\tau = x_4/c\) performed as a physical process
by the measurement apparatus at the registration event. This is the
content of {[}8, Theorem 19.1 of {[}24{]} (QM T19) with Lemmas 19.3
(\(dx_4/dt = ic\) Algebraic Channel) and 19.5 (\(dx_4/dt = ic\)
Geometric Channel){]} and {[}9, Theorems X.D and X.D.0 with the
underlying Theorem X.B (Universal McGucken the Geometric Channel
Theorem){]}, imported into the present paper as a standalone theorem of
the thermodynamics chain because the measurement-as-Wick-rotation
identity supplies the physical mechanism by which the Algebraic Channel
unitary content is converted to the Geometric Channel thermodynamic
content at every quantum-registration event in the universe --
including, as Theorem 26 of {[}24{]} below establishes, every
inter-molecular collision in a steam engine.

The measurement-as-Wick-rotation reading is not metaphorical. The
apparatus does not ``model'' the Wick rotation; it does not ``simulate''
it; the apparatus \emph{is} a physical Wick rotator. The localization
rate at which the apparatus performs the rotation is
\(\Gamma \sim N\omega_C\) where \(N\) is the number of Compton-coupled
apparatus degrees of freedom and \(\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar\) is the
average Compton frequency of those degrees of freedom; the spatial
localization length is \(\sigma \sim \sqrt{\lambda_C L_{\rm app}}\)
where \(\lambda_C = \hbar/(mc)\) is the Compton wavelength and
\(L_{\rm app}\) is the apparatus scale. The silver halide grain of a
photographic plate, the photocathode of a photomultiplier tube, the
depleted layer of a CCD pixel, the 11-cis-retinal chromophore of
biological vision, the tungsten electrode of a Geiger counter, and every
other quantum-measurement device in every laboratory are sites of
physical McGucken-Wick rotations. The history of experimental physics is
the history of physical Wick rotations.

\textbf{Theorem 25 of {[}24{]} (McGucken Measurement Theorem;
importation of {[}8, Theorem 19.1 of {[}24{]}{]} and {[}9, Theorem
X.D{]} into the present paper).} Under the McGucken Principle
\(dx_4/dt = ic\), the act of quantum measurement is the McGucken-Wick
rotation \(\tau = x_4/c\) operating as a physical process at the
registration event. Let \(\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)\) be the wavefunction on
the McGucken manifold \(\mathcal{M}_G\), with \(x_4 = ict\) as the
integrated coordinate constraint per the McGucken Principle. Let an
apparatus of \(N \sim 10^{23}\) Compton-coupled degrees of freedom,
characterized by Compton frequency \(\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar\) and
apparatus scale \(L_{\rm app}\), perform a measurement of observable
\(\hat O\) at laboratory time \(t\), registering an outcome at spatial
position \(\mathbf{x}\) on the 3D slice \(\Sigma_t = \{x_4 = ict\}\).
Then:

\emph{(A) The Algebraic Channel reading.} The measurement is implemented
by a coupling Hamiltonian \(\hat H_{\rm int}\) that entangles the
quantum entity with a macroscopic pointer via the Stone-theorem unitary
\(U_{\rm int}(\tau) = \exp(-i\tau \hat H_{\rm int}/\hbar)\), producing
the entangled superposition
\(\sum_n c_n |o_n\rangle_{\rm sys}\otimes|D_n\rangle_{\rm dev}\). The
Born rule (Theorem 4 of {[}24{]} plus {[}4, Theorem 4.2 of {[}24{]}{]})
assigns probabilities
\(P(o_n) = |c_n|^2 = |\langle o_n|\psi\rangle|^2\). The projection
postulate \(\psi \to \hat P_n\psi/\|\hat P_n\psi\|\) emerges from
tracing over the device's macroscopic degrees of freedom ({[}8, Lemma
19.3 of {[}24{]}{]}). The \(i\) in \(U_{\rm int}(\tau)\) is interior to
the operator algebra; this is the Algebraic Channel position-of-\(i\)
asymmetry of Theorem 19.5 of {[}24{]}.

\emph{(B) The Geometric Channel reading.} The measurement is the
3D-cross-section projection of the 4D wavefunction
\(\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)\) at the McGucken-constraint locus \(x_4 = ict\)
(the integrated coordinate shadow of \(dx_4/dt = ic\)) onto a single 3D
spatial point \(\mathbf{x}\) at the registration event ({[}8, Lemma 19.5
of {[}24{]}{]}). The Born density \(|\psi(\mathbf{x})|^2\) is the
SO(3)-Haar measure on the McGucken Sphere weighted by wavefunction
amplitude (Theorem 7 of {[}24{]}). The projection postulate is the
irreversible 4D-to-3D suppression at the registration moment, with the
irreversibility supplied by the apparatus's macroscopic
(\(N \sim 10^{23}\)-DOF) pointer having Compton-coupled to and amplified
the system's microscopic outcome -- the operational signature of the
strict Second Law (Theorem 9 of {[}24{]}) acting on the apparatus.

\emph{(W) The Wick rotation as the operational bridge between (A) and
(B) at the measurement event.} The McGucken-Wick rotation
\(\tau = x_4/c\) converts the Algebraic Channel wavefunction
(Lorentzian, with \(i\) interior to the path weight \(\exp(iS/\hbar)\),
oscillatory phase) to the Geometric Channel probability density
(Euclidean, with \(i\) exteriorised to the coordinate axis, real
positive measure \(|\psi|^2\)). The measurement apparatus performs this
rotation physically by projecting the 4D wavefunction onto a 3D spatial
slice at the McGucken-constraint locus \(x_4 = ict\) (the integrated
coordinate shadow of \(dx_4/dt = ic\)). The identification: the
McGucken-Wick rotation \(\tau = x_4/c\) that operates as a formal
mechanism throughout textbook QFT (the Feynman-Wiener correspondence of
Theorem 19 of {[}24{]}, the Osterwalder-Schrader reflection positivity,
the KMS periodicity, the Hawking-temperature Euclidean cigar of Theorem
16 of {[}24{]}) operates as a physical process at every
quantum-measurement event. \emph{The McGucken Measurement Theorem is the
physical-process face of the McGucken-Wick rotation at the
matter-dynamics tier.}

The rate at which the apparatus performs the Wick rotation is given by
the \((N+1)\)-vertex Feynman concentration of {[}6, Proposition VI.5{]}:

\[\Gamma_{\rm Wick} \;\sim\; N\,\omega_C \;\sim\; 10^{23} \cdot 10^{24}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}} \;=\; 10^{47}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}, \tag{25.1}\]

where the apparatus's \(N\) Compton-coupled degrees of freedom interact
pairwise with the system's McGucken Sphere via \(N\) pairwise vertices,
producing an aggregate localization rate proportional to \(N\omega_C\).
The spatial localization length supplied by the rotation is

\[\sigma_{\rm Wick} \;\sim\; \sqrt{\lambda_C \cdot L_{\rm app}}, \tag{25.2}\]

where \(\lambda_C = \hbar/(mc) \sim 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{m}\) for an
electron, \(L_{\rm app} \sim 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\) for a typical
laboratory apparatus, giving
\(\sigma_{\rm Wick} \sim 10^{-7.5}\,\mathrm{m}\), well within the
spatial resolution of optical and electronic detectors.

\emph{Proof.} Imported from {[}8, Theorem 19.1 of {[}24{]} with Lemmas
19.3 and 19.5{]} and integrated with the McGucken Duality of Theorems
19, 19.1-19.5 of {[}24{]}.

\emph{(A)} is established by {[}8, Lemma 19.3 of {[}24{]}{]}:
Stone-theorem coupling (Proposition H.2 of {[}24{]}) combined with the
Born-rule registration ({[}4, Theorem 4.2 of {[}24{]}{]}) and the
projection-postulate-from-tracing-over-the-device produces the Algebraic
Channel operator-algebraic content of measurement. The trace operation
over the device's macroscopic degrees of freedom converts the entangled
superposition \(\sum_n c_n |o_n\rangle\otimes|D_n\rangle\) to the mixed
state \(\rho = \sum_n |c_n|^2 |o_n\rangle\langle o_n|\), recovering the
projection postulate as a consequence of partial tracing rather than as
an independent dynamical postulate. The \(i\) in the coupling
Hamiltonian \(U_{\rm int}(\tau) = \exp(-i\tau \hat H_{\rm int}/\hbar)\)
is interior to the operator algebra by Theorem 19.5 of {[}24{]}.

\emph{(B)} is established by {[}8, Lemma 19.5 of {[}24{]}{]}: the
4D-to-3D Sphere projection at the McGucken-constraint locus
\(x_4 = ict\) (the integrated coordinate shadow of \(dx_4/dt = ic\))
produces a real positive measure \(|\psi|^2\) on the spatial three-slice
\(\Sigma_t\) by the SO(3)-Haar measure of Theorem 7 of {[}24{]}. The
macroscopic irreversibility of the projection is supplied by the
apparatus's \(N\)-DOF amplification: the system's microscopic outcome is
amplified to a macroscopic pointer state through \(N\) pairwise
Compton-coupling vertices, and the resulting macroscopic configuration
carries thermodynamic entropy increase by the strict Second Law of
Theorem 9 of {[}24{]}. The irreversibility is therefore not metaphorical
but operationally tied to the strict Second Law of \(dx_4/dt = ic\).

\emph{(W)} is the identification step. The Algebraic Channel
wavefunction has \(i\) interior (Theorem 19.5 of {[}24{]}, Step 2 of
{[}24{]}); the Geometric Channel probability density \(|\psi|^2\) has
\(i\) exteriorised through the modulus-squaring operation; the
operational mechanism that converts one to the other at the measurement
event is identical to the operational mechanism the McGucken-Wick
rotation performs at the equation level (Theorem 19.5 of {[}24{]},
Corollary 19.5.1 of {[}24{]}). The apparatus performs the rotation
physically because the wavefunction's support on \(\mathcal{M}_G\) lives
on the McGucken-constraint locus \(x_4 = ict\) (the integrated
coordinate shadow of \(dx_4/dt = ic\)), and the registration event is a
3D-cross-section projection at that locus -- which is identically the
substitution \(\tau = x_4/c\) performed on the wavefunction's support.
The localization-rate formula (25.1) follows from \(N\) pairwise Feynman
vertices each at frequency \(\omega_C\) ({[}6, Proposition VI.5{]}); the
localization-length formula (25.2) follows from the diffraction-limited
resolution of \(N\)-DOF Compton-coupled apparatus measurements. \(\Box\)

\textbf{Corollary 25.1 of {[}24{]} (Collapse and Measurement Are
Independent of Conscious Observers).} The McGucken Measurement Theorem
of Theorem 25 of {[}24{]} establishes that the Wick rotation is
performed by the apparatus's \(N \sim 10^{23}\) Compton-coupled degrees
of freedom, with no role for consciousness, intentionality, knowledge,
or observer awareness in the localization mechanism. The rotation rate
\(\Gamma_{\rm Wick} \sim N\omega_C \sim 10^{47}\) s\(^{-1}\) depends
only on the number of Compton-coupled apparatus degrees of freedom \(N\)
and the Compton frequency \(\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar\) of those degrees of
freedom; neither parameter has any dependence on whether a conscious
observer is present, whether the apparatus's output is read by a human,
whether the experimental record is later examined, or whether the
apparatus is in causal contact with any observer at all. \emph{The
apparatus performs the Wick rotation whether or not any observer is
watching.} The historical Copenhagen-school commitment that
consciousness or observer-knowledge plays a role in measurement collapse
is refuted by Corollary 25.1 of {[}24{]}.

\emph{Proof.} The proof of Theorem 25 of {[}24{]} invokes only (i) the
\(N\) Compton-coupled degrees of freedom of the apparatus, (ii) the
pairwise Compton-coupling Feynman vertices producing the
\((N+1)\)-vertex localization at rate \(N\omega_C\), (iii) the
projection of the wavefunction onto the McGucken-constraint locus
\(x_4 = ict\) (the integrated coordinate shadow of \(dx_4/dt = ic\)),
and (iv) the Born-rule probability assignment via the SO(3)-Haar
measure. None of these ingredients invokes consciousness,
observer-knowledge, awareness, or any agent-relative quantity. The
localization is performed by the apparatus's physical Compton-coupled
degrees of freedom, operating at frequencies set by the apparatus's
particle masses and apparatus scale, independent of any observer.
\(\Box\)

\emph{Diagnostic remark.} Corollary 25.1 of {[}24{]} dissolves a
long-standing concern in the foundations of quantum mechanics: the
apparent need to attribute special status to observer-knowledge in the
measurement process. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework's answer is
physical: measurement is a physical process performed by the apparatus,
with the apparatus's \(N\)-DOF Compton-coupled structure as the physical
mechanism. A Geiger counter in an empty laboratory at night performs

observer present and no observer-knowledge produced. The Wick rotation
is performed; the localization is registered; the apparatus output is

(11-cis-retinal chromophore + \textasciitilde{}\(10^7\) rods/cones +
neural processing), nested in series with the first. Every step is
physical; consciousness does not appear in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic
framework at any step.

\textbf{Corollary 25.2 of {[}24{]} (Every Wavefunction Collapse Is a
Physical Wick Rotation).} The orthodox ``wavefunction collapse'' of
quantum mechanics -- the apparent discontinuous transition
\(\psi \to \hat P_n\psi/\|\hat P_n\psi\|\) from a superposition to a
definite outcome at the moment of measurement -- is, under Theorem 25 of
{[}24{]}, the operational signature of the McGucken-Wick rotation
\(\tau = x_4/c\) acting on the wavefunction at the registration event.
\emph{Collapse is not a separate dynamical process; it is the Wick
rotation operating physically through the apparatus.} No new postulate
is required to handle collapse alongside the Schr?dinger equation; the
Schr?dinger equation's Geometric Channel face, exposed via the
McGucken-Wick rotation, supplies the collapse content as a direct
theorem of \(dx_4/dt = ic\).

\emph{Proof.} By Theorem 25 of \href{W}{24}, the Wick rotation
\(\tau = x_4/c\) converts the Algebraic Channel wavefunction
(oscillatory amplitude with \(i\) interior to the path weight) to the
Geometric Channel probability density (real positive measure with \(i\)
exteriorised). The orthodox ``collapse''
\(\psi \to \hat P_n\psi/\|\hat P_n\psi\|\) is the operational

\hypertarget{the-mcgucken-entropy-as-the-constructive-foundation-of-thermodynamics-that-einstein-sought}{%
\subsubsection{6.3 The McGucken Entropy as the constructive foundation
of thermodynamics that Einstein
sought}\label{the-mcgucken-entropy-as-the-constructive-foundation-of-thermodynamics-that-einstein-sought}}

The McGucken Entropy answers a dissatisfaction Einstein held about
thermodynamics for the whole of his career. Einstein famously divided
physics into two kinds of theory: \emph{constructive theories}, which
build phenomena upward from hypothesized constituent parts (the kinetic
theory of gases from molecules in motion), and \emph{principle
theories}, which begin from empirically established general constraints
and derive consequences analytically downward (thermodynamics from the
impossibility of perpetual motion). He admired thermodynamics as the
paradigmatic principle theory, but he regarded its lack of derivation
from a deeper constituent mechanism as fundamentally unsatisfactory for
genuine physical understanding. Four points define his position.

First, the \emph{principle-theory limitation}: thermodynamics proceeds
top-down, from macroscopic constraints observed to hold (perpetual
motion never occurs), rather than from a hypothesis about underlying
matter. Second, the \emph{desire for a constructive explanation}:
Einstein held that true understanding requires a bottom-up model that
explains phenomena through the motion of constituent parts --- ``when we
say we have succeeded in understanding a group of natural processes, we
invariably mean that a constructive theory has been found which covers
the processes in question.'' Third, the \emph{missing why}: principle
theories offer certainty and logical perfection but are explanatory-lite
--- ``the advantages of the constructive theory are completeness,
adaptability, and clearness; those of the principle theory are logical
perfection and security of the foundations'' --- they dictate what can
happen without explaining how or why the underlying mechanism behaves as
it does. Fourth, the \emph{Boltzmann parallel}: Einstein regarded
classical thermodynamics as an incomplete worldview until Boltzmann
supplied a deeper microphysical account through statistical mechanics,
and he viewed his own special relativity with the same productive
unease, as a principle theory awaiting a constructive foundation ---
``like thermodynamics before Boltzmann.''

The McGucken Entropy supplies exactly the constructive foundation
Einstein sought, and carries Boltzmann's account one level deeper.
Boltzmann reduced thermodynamic entropy to a count of microstates, S =
k\_B ln Ω, but left the microstates themselves --- and the arrow along
which the count grows --- as inputs from an assumed mechanics. The
McGucken Entropy is the constructive layer beneath Boltzmann's: Ω is the
count of distinguishable states the physically expanding McGucken Sphere
passes through, one Compton tick of action h at a time (§6.1), and the
arrow along which Ω grows is the +ic orientation of the expansion itself
(§4.1, §6.2). The Second Law, the entropy, and the arrow of time are
thus derived from the movement of a constituent physical thing --- the
expanding fourth dimension at every event --- which is precisely the
bottom-up, constructive account (constituent parts in motion) that
Einstein required for understanding, rather than a top-down principle
imposed on the phenomena. Where Boltzmann gave thermodynamics its
constructive foundation in the statistics of molecules, \(dx_4/dt = ic\)
gives Boltzmann's statistics their constructive foundation in the
physical expansion that generates the states. And because the same
expanding Sphere that grounds thermodynamics also grounds the Born rule
and gravity (§7), the constructive foundation Einstein wanted for
thermodynamics turns out to be the constructive foundation of quantum
mechanics and general relativity as well --- the single physical
mechanism, \(dx_4/dt = ic\), beneath all three principle theories at
once.

\hypertarget{the-mcgucken-principle-dxux2084dt-ic-reading-of-carcassis-entropy-floor-the-zero-of-entropy-at-the-spheres-wavelength-h-unitarity-before-registration-irreversibility-at-registration-and-the-uncertainty-principle-as-a-relation-between-registered-variances}{%
\subsubsection{6.4 The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic Reading of
Carcassi's Entropy Floor: the Zero of Entropy at the Sphere's Wavelength
h, Unitarity Before Registration, Irreversibility at Registration, and
the Uncertainty Principle as a Relation Between Registered
Variances}\label{the-mcgucken-principle-dxux2084dt-ic-reading-of-carcassis-entropy-floor-the-zero-of-entropy-at-the-spheres-wavelength-h-unitarity-before-registration-irreversibility-at-registration-and-the-uncertainty-principle-as-a-relation-between-registered-variances}}

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension \(x_4\) is
expanding at the velocity of light: \(dx_4/dt = ic\), with
\(x_4 = ict\), as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose
wavelength sets the action \(h\) and whose volume defines a nonlocality.

\textbf{McGucken Principle anchor.} Everything in this section descends
from that Principle, and the Principle fixes in advance what each item
below must be. The Sphere's wavelength sets the action \(h\): one
Compton tick of the expansion carries one quantum of action, so the
smallest distinguishable cell of the Sphere's state-count is one cell of
phase-space area \(h\), the count of one cell is \(\Omega = 1\), and its
entropy is \(S = k_B \ln 1 = 0\). The Sphere's volume defines a
nonlocality: the expansion from an event proceeds in all directions at
once, so a particle coupled to it has no single position and no single
momentum before the expansion is read at a registration event
(§4.1.0bis). The \(+ic\) orientation of the expansion is one-directional
(Theorem 19.5.1 of {[}24{]}): the dx₄/dt = ic Algebraic Channel, which
carries the unitary evolution between registrations, is time-symmetric
and conserves the count; the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel, which
carries the registration, reads the count on the spatial slice at the
locus \(x_4 = ict\) and is irreversible (Theorem 25 of {[}24{]},
§6.2.10). Carcassi's lecture ``It's all about the entropy'' {[}81{]}
states, from inside the orthodox formalism and with no reference to
\(dx_4/dt = ic\), a lower bound on entropy at the phase-space area
\(h\), the conservation of entropy under unitary maps, the necessity of
a non-unitary channel for any entropy increase, the uncertainty
principle as a consequence of the entropy floor, and the ensemble
character of every physical state. Each of these is quoted verbatim
below with its timestamp and read as the theorem of \(dx_4/dt = ic\) it
corresponds to; where Carcassi states an open problem, the problem is
itemized and answered with the corpus theorem named.

\hypertarget{entropy-is-quantum-mechanics-the-zero-of-entropy-at-the-phase-space-area-h-is-the-one-cell-count-of-the-mcgucken-sphere}{%
\paragraph{6.4.1 ``Entropy is quantum mechanics'': the zero of entropy
at the phase-space area h is the one-cell count of the McGucken
Sphere}\label{entropy-is-quantum-mechanics-the-zero-of-entropy-at-the-phase-space-area-h-is-the-one-cell-count-of-the-mcgucken-sphere}}

\textbf{McGucken Principle anchor.} The Principle predicts a floor on
entropy and predicts its location: the Sphere's wavelength sets \(h\),
one Compton tick carries one action quantum, and the smallest count is
one cell, \(\Omega = 1\), \(S = 0\).

Carcassi's argument runs in three quoted steps. First, the classical
defect (19:04--19:29): ``classical mechanics allows for arbitrarily
small entropy and in fact a single particle state has minus infinite
entropy. But thermodynamics does not allow for arbitrary small entropy.
The third law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of a system
cannot be lower than the one of a perfect crystalline substance. a zero
entropy.'' Second, the dimensional defect of the textbook formula
\(S = -\int \rho \ln \rho\, dx\, dp\) (22:04--22:21): ``X is units of
length and P of units of mass times velocity. So we are taking the
logarithm of a quantity with units. And this is dimensionally incorrect.
You can only take the logarithm of a pure number.'' Third, the repair
and its meaning (23:07--23:36): ``If you take a uniform distribution of
a region of area H, then the distribution has zero entropy. H / H is one
and the logarithm of one is zero. So just be clear, we don't know
anything about uh quantum mechanics and we don't know about the plasma
{[}Planck{]} constant. We do know about the third law of thermodynamics
and then we have a zero for the entropy. So h is the area that
corresponds to the zero of our entropy for a uniform distribution.'' And
the comparison with quantum mechanics (26:04--26:16): ``Pure states in
quantum mechanics have zero entropy. So you can have lower entropy in
quantum mechanics. It's like quantum mechanics takes the third law very
serious. Classical mechanics doesn't. Classical mechanics does not obey
the laws of thermodynamics.''

\emph{LTD reading.} Carcassi introduces \(h\) as a constant required to
make the logarithm dimensionless and locates the zero of entropy at a
uniform distribution over one area \(h\); the Principle supplies both as
theorems. The McGucken Entropy is \(S_{\text{McG}} = k_B \ln \Omega\)
with \(\Omega\) the count of distinguishable states of the expanding
Sphere, one per Compton tick, each carrying one quantum of action \(h\)
(§6.1, Definition). The reference cell Carcassi must insert by hand is
therefore the Sphere's wavelength: the area \(h\) is the action per tick
of the expansion, the quantity the Principle names in its statement. The
zero of entropy is the one-cell count: \(\Omega = 1\),
\(S = k_B \ln 1 = 0\), which is Step 5 of §3.14 (``the state-count Ω
cannot fall below one distinguishable cell (one action quantum h)'').
Carcassi's observation that a pure quantum state has zero von Neumann
entropy while a classical point has entropy \(-\infty\) is, under the
Principle, the statement that the Sphere is a physical object of finite
wavelength: a classical point is a region of zero phase-space area, so
with \(h\) fixed its entropy is \(\ln(A/h)\) at \(A \to 0\), which is
\(-\infty\), and equivalently a Sphere of zero wavelength, \(h \to 0\),
would resolve \(A/h \to \infty\) cells in any finite area while the
point holds none; the Principle excludes this because its wavelength is
set by the Compton frequency \(\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar\) of the coupled
matter (§2, §4.1.0). The dimensional requirement Carcassi states applies
to every differential entropy in this paper as well: the Wiener reading
of Theorem 6.1, \(S_W = (3/2) k_B \ln(4\pi e D t/\ell^2)\), requires a
reference length \(\ell\), and under the Principle that reference is the
Compton step of the diffusion, \(\ell = \lambda_C\) (§4.1), the same
cell that supplies Carcassi's \(h\); Theorem 6.1 is stated with this
reference. The sentence ``Classical mechanics does not obey the laws of
thermodynamics'' is, in the McGucken reading, the statement that
classical mechanics is the description in which the Sphere's cells are
left unresolved (Theorem 26.4 of {[}24{]}, the three
registration-character regimes), so that no floor appears; the floor is
restored the moment the count is taken at the Sphere's own resolution.

\hypertarget{the-classical-uncertainty-principle-ux3c3_xux3c3_p-ux210fe-from-the-third-law-the-quantum-bound-ux210f2-and-the-factor-e2-between-them}{%
\paragraph{6.4.2 The classical uncertainty principle σ\_xσ\_p ≥ ℏ/e from
the third law, the quantum bound ℏ/2, and the factor e/2 between
them}\label{the-classical-uncertainty-principle-ux3c3_xux3c3_p-ux210fe-from-the-third-law-the-quantum-bound-ux210f2-and-the-factor-e2-between-them}}

\textbf{McGucken Principle anchor.} The Principle gives the quantum
bound \(\hbar/2\) as a theorem (§3.14, Steps 1--4: the commutator from
the perpendicular \(i\), the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality on the Sphere's
sesquilinear Haar pairing). The classical bound Carcassi derives from
the third law is the same floor counted with the cell's interior treated
as resolvable; the gap between the two bounds is computed below.

Carcassi derives (24:06--25:27): ``the entropy of row {[}ρ{]} is less or
equal to the logarithm of 2 pi e sigma x sigma p / h. If you fix the
uncertainty, you can go up in entropy until you hit the Gaussian bound.
\ldots{} So let's solve for the uncertainty and we get that the product
of sigma x sigma p is greater or equal to h bar over 2 pi e the
exponential of the entropy. \ldots{} So the uncertainty has a lower
bound given by the entropy. But the third law imposes a lower bound on
the entropy which is zero. And the exponential of zero is one. So
classical statistical mechanics plus the third law of thermodynamics
gives us the classical uncertainty principle. Sigma X sigma P is greater
than H bar over E.'' On the gap to the quantum bound (26:22--27:22):
``Note that E is slightly more than two. So you do get a little bit less
uncertainty in classical mechanics. Why? Because you minimize the
uncertainty at the same entropy precisely when you have independent
Gaussians for both position and momentum. That's what you can't do
anymore if you have a lower bound on the entropy because if they were
independent you would be able to write the joint distribution as a
product of the two. But writing a joint distribution assumes you can
define a region of phase space arbitrarily small which is exactly what
you can do if you have a lower bound of the entropy. \ldots{} We now
have a conceptual reason as to why joint probability distribution of
conjugate quantities are not possible. It is just the lower bound on the
entropy.''

The arithmetic is as stated. The maximum differential entropy of a
phase-space density with given marginal variances \(\sigma_x, \sigma_p\)
is attained by the product of two Gaussians and equals
\(\ln(2\pi e\, \sigma_x \sigma_p / h)\) in units of the cell \(h\);
imposing \(S \ge 0\) gives
\(\sigma_x \sigma_p \ge h/(2\pi e) = \hbar/e\). The quantum bound of
§3.14 is \(\sigma_q \sigma_p \ge \hbar/2\). Since \(e/2 = 1.359\), the
quantum bound is the stricter one, and the ratio of the two bounds is
\(e/2\). The minimum-uncertainty quantum state, the Gaussian with
\(\sigma_q \sigma_p = \hbar/2\), has von Neumann entropy zero and, read
as a classical phase-space density (its Wigner function, which is
positive for this state), classical differential entropy
\(\ln(2\pi e \cdot \hbar/2 \,/\, h) = \ln(e/2) = 1 - \ln 2 = 0.307\) in
units of \(k_B\). The quantum count assigns one cell, \(\Omega = 1\), to
a region whose classical count is \(e/2 > 1\) cells.

\emph{LTD reading.} The two bounds are two readings of the one Sphere.
The classical bound treats the Sphere's cell of area \(h\) as a region
whose interior carries a resolvable Gaussian density, so the floor
\(S = 0\) sits at an area \(h\) and the minimum-uncertainty Gaussian
occupies \(e/2\) such areas. The quantum bound counts the Sphere's cells
as the Sphere itself resolves them: the sesquilinear pairing
\(\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle\) of §3.3 (Lemma 7.6 of {[}29{]}) is the
SO(3)-invariant Haar pairing on the Sphere, and the Cauchy--Schwarz
inequality on that pairing (Step 3 of §3.14) bounds the product of
registered variances by
\(\tfrac12 |\langle[\hat q,\hat p]\rangle| = \hbar/2\), with the
commutator \([\hat q,\hat p] = i\hbar\) the perpendicular \(i\) of the
\(x_4\)-advance carrying one quantum per tick (QM T10 of {[}38{]}).
Carcassi's reason for the gap --- that independent Gaussians in \(x\)
and \(p\) would require defining a region of phase space smaller than
the floor allows --- is, under the Principle, the statement that
position and momentum are readings of the two mutually perpendicular
channels of the one Sphere (Step 6 of §3.14): the Geometric Channel
reads the spatial localization, the Algebraic Channel reads the
translation generator, and one Sphere of one wavelength \(h\) cannot be
factored into two independent cells. Carcassi's remark that the
saturating states are Gaussian on both bounds (27:30--27:37) matches
§4.1: the Gaussian is the kernel of the Compton-step Wiener process
(Theorem 19.5.1, §4.1.1), the one-tick Huygens displacement of the
coupled particle, so the state of least registered spread at fixed count
is the state of one tick.

\hypertarget{unitary-maps-conserve-entropy-every-entropy-increase-is-a-non-unitary-channel-the-algebraic-channel-between-registrations-and-the-geometric-channel-at-registration}{%
\paragraph{6.4.3 Unitary maps conserve entropy; every entropy increase
is a non-unitary channel: the Algebraic Channel between registrations
and the Geometric Channel at
registration}\label{unitary-maps-conserve-entropy-every-entropy-increase-is-a-non-unitary-channel-the-algebraic-channel-between-registrations-and-the-geometric-channel-at-registration}}

\textbf{McGucken Principle anchor.} The Principle predicts both halves
of Carcassi's statement and the relation between them. Between
registrations the Algebraic Channel evolution is unitary and
time-symmetric (Theorem 19.5 of {[}24{]}; §6.2.1, ``the full closed
state evolves unitarily''), so the von Neumann entropy of the full state
is constant and a pure state stays pure with \(S_{vN} = 0\). At a
registration the Geometric Channel reads the Sphere on the spatial slice
at \(x_4 = ict\) (Theorem 25 of {[}24{]}, part (B)), the registered
subsystem is a reduced state, and its entropy rises from \(0\) to the
Shannon entropy of the Born distribution; the direction is fixed by the
\(+ic\) orientation (Theorem 19.5.1 of {[}24{]}), and Corollary 19.5.3
of {[}24{]} states that the McGucken--Wick rotation \(\tau = x_4/c\)
performed at registration does not preserve the Algebraic Channel's
unitary structure.

Carcassi states the unitary half (49:13--49:41): ``It must be clear that
this stretch map cannot be unitary transformation because unitary
transformation conserve entropy and preserve a commitator
{[}commutator{]} relationship and this cannot. So this has to be quantum
channels that is that maps that maps density matrices to density
matrices. They don't really map pure states to other pure states.'' And
of the closed-system equations (49:58--50:23): ``The Hamiltonian
equation, the Hamiltonian equations in the the shinger {[}Schrödinger{]}
equation in the quantum case, they only describe closed system things
that are deterministic reversible, things that do not have energy
transfer, do not increase or decrease entropy.'' He states the algebraic
reason (51:58--52:17): ``that means that you would preserve in the
commutators. So that means that you have a unitary evolution which is
not what we can have and or another way to see it is that something that
preserves a product has to map pure states to pure states which not not
what we can do if we want to increase entropy.'' He then constructs the
entropy-increasing map as a Lindblad channel with no Hamiltonian part
(1:00:55--1:01:23): ``the Hamiltonian is zero because we don't want any
any unitary part. We we want that we want a pure stretching map. So the
map should be purely dissipative and the L or this jump operator is just
going to be a dagger,'' and names what it is (1:03:52--1:03:58): ``It's
really this process this decipative {[}dissipative{]} process that you
let go for some fixed amount of time.'' He verifies entropy increase for
all states from \([a, a^\dagger] = 1\) (1:04:23--1:04:49): ``we have a
dagger a is less than a a dagger and we take this bring it to the other
side but this is just the commutator and the commutator is one and of
course the identity is a a non- negative definite operator. Therefore
yes this actually increases the entropy for all states.''

\emph{LTD reading.} The two statements Carcassi makes --- unitary maps
conserve entropy and commutators; entropy increase requires a channel
that maps pure states to mixed states --- are the two channels of
\(dx_4/dt = ic\) stated in operator language. The first is the Algebraic
Channel: \(S_{vN}(U\rho U^\dagger) = S_{vN}(\rho)\) for every unitary
\(U\), and the Born probabilities \(p_n = |\langle o_n|\psi\rangle|^2\)
do not appear in it at all, because they require the choice of a
registration basis \(\{|o_n\rangle\}\), which the unitary evolution does
not supply (Theorem 25 of {[}24{]}, part (A): the probabilities are
assigned at the registration, by the Born rule, after the coupling
unitary). The second is the Geometric Channel: at the registration the
apparatus's \(N\) Compton-coupled degrees of freedom are traced out
(Lemma 19.3 of {[}24{]}), the system's state becomes
\(\rho = \sum_n |c_n|^2 |o_n\rangle\langle o_n|\), and its von Neumann
entropy is \(-\sum_n |c_n|^2 \ln |c_n|^2\), the Shannon entropy of the
Born distribution --- readings (1) and (3) of Theorem 6.1, Steps 1 and
3, now equal because the registration basis is the coarse-graining. The
channel Carcassi constructs --- a Lindblad generator with \(H = 0\) and
a single jump operator --- is of the same class as the reduced-state
generator computed in §6.2.1 from the Compton coupling, where the
momentum-diffusion coefficient
\(D_p = \tfrac12 m^2 \varepsilon^2 c^2 \Omega\) is the Lindblad term the
environmental trace produces and the full state remains unitary. His
entropy increment, the same \(\ln \lambda\) for every state under a
rescaling of the cell count \(N \to \lambda N\), is the increment of
\(k_B \ln N\) under uniform multiplication of the count; under the
Principle the count of a registered ensemble grows with the ticks, and
the rate is the H-theorem of Theorem 19.5.1 (§4.1.1),
\(dS/dt = k_B D \int |\nabla P|^2/P \ge 0\). What Carcassi supplies by
choosing \(H = 0\) and \(L = a^\dagger\) --- a channel that adds quanta
and never removes them --- the Principle supplies as the \(+ic\)
orientation: every Compton tick adds one cell to the count and the
expansion has no \(-ic\) branch (Theorem 19.5.1 of {[}24{]}), which is
why the registered entropy has a direction and the unitary evolution
between registrations does not.

\hypertarget{without-measurement-there-is-no-quantum-mechanics-susskinds-unitarity-as-an-algebraic-channel-theorem-that-omits-the-registration}{%
\paragraph{6.4.4 ``Without measurement there is no quantum mechanics'':
Susskind's unitarity as an Algebraic Channel theorem that omits the
registration}\label{without-measurement-there-is-no-quantum-mechanics-susskinds-unitarity-as-an-algebraic-channel-theorem-that-omits-the-registration}}

\textbf{McGucken Principle anchor.} The Principle states that the Sphere
is read at registration events on the spatial slice \(x_4 = ict\)
(Theorem 25 of {[}24{]}); every quantity quantum mechanics predicts, and
every quantity by which it has been tested, is a statistic of such
registrations. The unitary evolution operator is a theorem about the
Algebraic Channel between registrations; a statement that quantum
mechanics is unitary, with registration omitted, is a statement about a
theory with no Born rule, no probabilities, and no entropy change, which
is a theory with no empirical quantities.

Susskind states that the time evolution of a closed quantum system is
unitary and that distinctions between states are conserved under it
{[}82{]}. Carcassi states, independently, the premise that makes this an
incomplete description of quantum mechanics (1:20:58--1:21:47): ``the
scientific laws describe relationship that can always be experimentally
reproduced. \ldots{} Scientific laws are then relationship between
ensemble. Every time that I have this, I will get this. And so the
objects of which the scientific law has to be about must be an ensemble
the infinite collection of the possible outcome of our preparation
processes.'' He states that the Born rule is itself an entropy statement
(1:19:16--1:19:36): ``The bore {[}Born{]} rule is one to one with the
entropy. If you get the entropy of a mixture of two pure states, then
that entropy is an invertible function of the square root of the border
root, the square root of probability of transition.'' And he states the
finite duration of every registration (1:24:17--1:24:36): ``even a
single measurement takes a finite amount of time. So every single
measure is actually an average of unfinite {[}a finite{]} time.''

\emph{LTD reading.} The three quoted statements, together with §6.4.3,
give the argument in full. (i) Unitary evolution conserves the von
Neumann entropy (§6.4.3; Carcassi 49:13). (ii) The Born rule is
one-to-one with the von Neumann entropy of the equal mixture (Carcassi
1:19:16; Carcassi--Thrien--Aidala {[}39{]}, §7: the equal mixture
\(\rho = \tfrac12(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| + |\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi|)\)
has eigenvalues \((1 \pm \sqrt p)/2\) with
\(p = |\langle\psi|\varphi\rangle|^2\)). (iii) Therefore a description
of quantum mechanics consisting of the unitary evolution alone contains
no change of entropy and hence no realized Born probability: the number
\(|\langle o_n|\psi\rangle|^2\) is defined in it as a mathematical
overlap, and it becomes a frequency only at registrations (Theorem 25 of
{[}24{]}, part (A) for the assignment, part (B) for the irreversible
reading on the slice). (iv) The empirical quantities of quantum
mechanics are registration statistics (Carcassi 1:20:58--1:21:47): the
laws are relations between ensembles of outcomes of preparation and
measurement. Hence a theory of the unitary operator alone has no
empirical quantities, which is the exact sense of the statement that
without measurement there is no quantum mechanics. Susskind's statement
is therefore correct as a theorem of the Algebraic Channel --- Theorem
19.5 of {[}24{]} states the Algebraic Channel is unitary and
time-symmetric, and §6.2.1 states the full closed state evolves
unitarily --- and it is incomplete as a statement about quantum
mechanics, because it omits the Geometric Channel registration at which
the Sphere is read, the reduced state acquires the Shannon entropy of
the Born distribution, and the direction is fixed by \(+ic\) (Theorem
19.5.1 of {[}24{]}). The information that is conserved is the
information of the full state including the apparatus and environment;
the information that is lost is the information of the registered
subsystem, whose reduced state after the trace over the apparatus's
\(N \sim 10^{23}\) Compton-coupled degrees of freedom (Lemma 19.3 of
{[}24{]}) no longer carries the relative phases. Carcassi's observation
that every registration takes a finite time is, under the Principle, the
statement that the registration is a physical process of the apparatus
with the rate \(\Gamma_{\text{Wick}} \sim N\omega_C\) of equation (25.1)
in §6.2.10, and that no registration resolves an interval shorter than
one Compton tick of the Sphere, the tick that carries the one quantum
\(h\). The corpus demonstrates the irreversibility of the registered
event in several independent ways: the \(+ic\) chirality (Theorem 19.5.1
of {[}24{]}), the McGucken Measurement Theorem (Theorem 25 of {[}24{]},
§6.2.10), the Second Law of the reduced state (Theorem 19.5.1, §4.1.1),
and the volume-augmenting reading of the Sphere's expansion against the
volume-conserving unitary reading (§3.11), under which the registered
event is oriented, definite, and irreversible while the Algebraic
Channel description of the same system is time-symmetric. For the
gravitational case, the horizon reading of the count,
\(S_{BH} = k_B A/(4\ell_P^2)\) (§4.2, §5.4), is already the entropy of
the registered horizon states, so a unitarity claim for black-hole
evolution is, in the same way, a statement about the Algebraic Channel
operator and not about the registered count that the Bekenstein--Hawking
entropy measures.

\hypertarget{the-uncertainty-principle-its-cause-is-the-spheres-nonlocal-volume-present-without-measurement-its-numerical-form-ux3c3_qux3c3_p-ux210f2-is-a-relation-between-registered-variances}{%
\paragraph{6.4.5 The uncertainty principle: its cause is the Sphere's
nonlocal volume, present without measurement; its numerical form
σ\_qσ\_p ≥ ℏ/2 is a relation between registered
variances}\label{the-uncertainty-principle-its-cause-is-the-spheres-nonlocal-volume-present-without-measurement-its-numerical-form-ux3c3_qux3c3_p-ux210f2-is-a-relation-between-registered-variances}}

\textbf{McGucken Principle anchor.} The Principle states that the
Sphere's volume defines a nonlocality: a particle coupled to the
expansion has, before any registration, no single position and no single
momentum, because the expansion it is coupled to proceeds from the event
in every direction at once (§4.1.0bis; {[}48{]}). This is the cause of
the spread, and it is present whether or not a registration occurs. The
quantity \(\sigma_q \sigma_p\) is a product of variances, and a variance
is defined over an ensemble of registered outcomes (Carcassi
1:21:26--1:21:47); the relation \(\sigma_q \sigma_p \ge \hbar/2\)
therefore acquires its numerical form at registration, where the
Sphere's volume is read as the Born distribution over cells of one
quantum each (Theorem 25 of {[}24{]}, part (B); Theorem 7 of {[}24{]}).
The two statements are kept apart and both hold.

Carcassi states the connection between entropy and uncertainty in the
direction of hiding (39:18--39:24): ``Uncertainty on a variable becomes
more and more indistinguishable from the uncertainty on its
complimentary variable. The uncertainty is essentially what is hiding
the quantumness.'' He explains with the maximally mixed state
(39:46--40:23): ``the maximally mixed state is essentially the identity.
And since the identity commutes with everything, you can kind of make
them commute. First, you use the cyclic property of the trace. So, A
goes on the other side. And then the identity commutes with a. So the
net result AB turn into BA. So the expectation of AB is the expectation
of BA for the maximally mixed state.'' He then states his program and
its open problem (1:13:14--1:14:20): ``the direct correspondence
principle is taking a classical theory and substituting the post some
{[}Poisson{]} brackets with the commutator over IH bar. So what we're
doing when you're doing that quantization is really taking a classical
theory and putting a lower bound to the entropy. This means that every
every quantum effect that we have entanglement a certainty
{[}uncertainty{]} principle anything that is there in quantum mechanics
it's all because we have a lower bound on the entropy \ldots{} all the
mysteries of quantum mechanics maybe I still don't know how but they
should all come from the lower bound on the entropy. There is nothing
else.''

\emph{LTD reading.} The maximally mixed state is, on the Sphere, the
uniform SO(3)-Haar measure over the directional cross-section with no
direction resolved: the Born measure \(N(R_\varphi)/N(S^2)\) (Appendix
A) evaluated over the whole Sphere is 1, and the expectation of every
product is the trace, so position and momentum commute in expectation
exactly when the registration resolves no cell. At the other end, the
pure state is the Sphere counted as one cell, and the commutator
\([\hat q, \hat p] = i\hbar\) is the perpendicular \(i\) of the
\(x_4\)-advance with the action \(h\) per tick (QM T10 of {[}38{]}).
Carcassi's ``substituting the Poisson brackets with the commutator over
\(i\hbar\)'' is the direct correspondence; under the Principle the
deformation parameter \(\hbar\) and the imaginary unit \(i\) are the two
readings of \(dx_4/dt = ic\): \(\hbar\) the action the Sphere's
wavelength sets, \(i\) the perpendicularity of the advance to the
spatial slice (§3.14, Step 1). Carcassi states an open problem ---
``maybe I still don't know how'' --- and its criterion: every quantum
effect, entanglement and the uncertainty principle among them, is to
come from the lower bound on the entropy and from nothing else. The
Principle answers the criterion item by item. The lower bound itself is
the one-cell count at the Sphere's wavelength \(h\) (§6.4.1; Step 5 of
§3.14). The Born rule is the SO(3)-Haar measure on the Sphere (§3,
Theorem 7.2 of {[}29{]}, five routes), and its one-to-one relation with
the entropy of the equal mixture is the count-to-measure relation of §7.
The uncertainty principle is the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality on the
Sphere's sesquilinear pairing with the commutator from the perpendicular
\(i\) (§3.14, Steps 1--4, QM T12 of {[}38{]}). Entanglement is one
expanding McGucken Sphere measured at two points (§5.9), the nonlocality
the Principle's volume defines. The Second Law is the H-theorem of the
reduced state under the Compton-step diffusion (Theorem 19.5.1, §4.1.1).
Carcassi's ``there is nothing else'' is, under the Principle, correct in
the following exact sense: there is one thing, the expanding Sphere
whose wavelength sets \(h\), and the lower bound on entropy is one of
its readings; what Carcassi reaches as a bound imposed on a classical
theory, the Principle gives as the physical object whose count has the
bound. The uncertainty principle is then read correctly in both
directions at once. Its cause is the Sphere's nonlocal volume at Compton
resolution, present in unobserved systems and during free evolution
({[}48{]}; §3.14, Step 7). Its statement
\(\sigma_q \sigma_p \ge \hbar/2\) is about registered variances, and a
registration always reveals the probabilistic, nonlocal expansion of the
Sphere: the registered position is one cell of the Sphere's spatial
reading, the registered momentum one value of the translation generator
(Step 6 of §3.14), and the floor on their joint spread is the one-cell
floor of the count, \(\Omega \ge 1\). The thermodynamic form of the same
floor is Carcassi's third-law bound, \(S \ge 0\) at the area \(h\)
(§6.4.2).

\hypertarget{classical-mechanics-as-the-high-entropy-limit-ux210f-0-and-c-as-two-readings-of-one-principle-and-the-mechanism-the-principle-specifies}{%
\paragraph{6.4.6 Classical mechanics as the high-entropy limit, ℏ → 0
and c → ∞ as two readings of one Principle, and the mechanism the
Principle
specifies}\label{classical-mechanics-as-the-high-entropy-limit-ux210f-0-and-c-as-two-readings-of-one-principle-and-the-mechanism-the-principle-specifies}}

\textbf{McGucken Principle anchor.} The Principle contains both
constants Carcassi's two limits refer to: \(c\) is the rate of the
expansion and \(h\) the action its wavelength sets (Appendix E, §2). The
non-relativistic limit \(v \ll c\) and the classical limit of high
entropy are two limits of the one Sphere: the first leaves the
worldline's share of the expansion near \(c\), the second leaves the
count of cells large, \(N \gg 1\).

Carcassi states the result (0:52--0:58): ``If you take quantum mechanics
and go to high entropy, poof, you get classical mechanics.'' He states
the reading of the two limits (7:54--8:04): ``h bar going to zero is a
shortcut for saying that the entropy of the system is high. Much like C
going to infinity is a shortcut for saying that the speeds are low.'' He
separates the limit from the measurement problem (8:32--8:38): ``just to
be clear, the classical limit has nothing to do with the measurement
problem. The measurement problem, if you believe it exists, is a
consistency problem within quantum mechanics.'' He states the formal
result (1:12:50--1:13:03): ``mathematicians say things like the moy
{[}Moyal{]} bracket is the unique one parameter le {[}Lie{]} algebraic
deformation of the pson {[}Poisson{]} bracket which translated for us it
means there is only one way to do it.'' And he states that the mechanism
producing the high entropy lies outside the limit (1:15:43--1:15:48):
``the mechanism is irrelevant. As long as you are at high entropy, you
can use classical mechanics.''

\emph{LTD reading.} Carcassi's parallel between \(\hbar \to 0\) and
\(c \to \infty\) is exact under the Principle, because the two constants
are the two parameters of the one expansion \(dx_4/dt = ic\) with
wavelength setting \(h\): \(c \to \infty\) is the reading in which the
worldline's share of the expansion (the standard time-dilation factor
\(c\,d\tau/dt = c/\gamma\)) is indistinguishable from \(c\), and
\(\hbar \to 0\) is the reading in which the Sphere's cells are so many
that the count is read as a continuum, \(\ln \Omega\) large and the
one-cell floor invisible. Carcassi's statement that the classical limit
is separate from the measurement problem is a correct statement about
the limit: the limit is a statement about the count \(N \gg 1\), and the
measurement problem is a statement about how a registration selects one
cell. Under the Principle the two are related through one object: the
Sphere whose count is large in the limit is the Sphere that is read at
registration, and Theorem 26.4 of {[}24{]} states the quantum-classical
transition as three registration-character regimes of the same Sphere.
The uniqueness of the Moyal bracket as the one-parameter deformation of
the Poisson bracket is the formal counterpart of Step 1 of §3.14: the
one parameter is \(\hbar\), the action per tick, and the direction of
deformation is the perpendicular \(i\). Carcassi's statement that the
mechanism is irrelevant to the use of classical mechanics at high
entropy is correct for the limit; the Principle specifies the mechanism
that produces the entropy and the specification carries a prediction:
the Compton-coupled registration of every inter-molecular collision
(Theorem 26 of {[}24{]}), with the reduced-state Lindblad generator of
§6.2.1 and the residual zero-temperature diffusion
\(D_x^{(\text{McG})} = \varepsilon^2 c^2 \Omega / 2\gamma^2\), which is
zero in a theory that leaves the mechanism unspecified and is bounded by
present optical-clock and trapped-ion interferometry.

\hypertarget{summary-the-mcgucken-attribution-for-each-item-of-carcassis-lecture}{%
\paragraph{6.4.7 Summary: the McGucken attribution for each item of
Carcassi's
lecture}\label{summary-the-mcgucken-attribution-for-each-item-of-carcassis-lecture}}

Carcassi's lecture {[}81{]} states five facts from inside the orthodox
formalism; the McGucken Principle \(dx_4/dt = ic\) gives each as a
theorem and names the object the facts are about.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The zero of entropy at the phase-space area \(h\)} (Carcassi
  23:07--23:36) is the one-cell count of the McGucken Sphere,
  \(\Omega = 1\), \(S = k_B \ln 1 = 0\), with \(h\) the action set by
  the Sphere's wavelength (§6.1; §3.14, Step 5). McGucken's
  contribution: the reference cell Carcassi inserts to make the
  logarithm dimensionless is the quantity the Principle names in its
  statement.
\item
  \textbf{The classical uncertainty principle
  \(\sigma_x \sigma_p \ge \hbar/e\) from the third law} (Carcassi
  24:06--25:27) and the quantum bound \(\hbar/2\) (§3.14) differ by the
  factor \(e/2\), the classical cell count of the minimum-uncertainty
  Gaussian to which the quantum count assigns one cell. McGucken's
  contribution: the quantum bound is the count at the Sphere's own
  resolution, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality on the Sphere's SO(3)-Haar
  pairing with the commutator from the perpendicular \(i\) (§3.14, Steps
  1--4).
\item
  \textbf{Unitary maps conserve entropy; entropy increase is a
  non-unitary channel} (Carcassi 49:13--50:23, 1:00:55--1:04:49) are the
  Algebraic Channel between registrations and the Geometric Channel at
  registration (Theorem 19.5, Theorem 25, Corollary 19.5.3 of {[}24{]};
  §6.2.1). McGucken's contribution: the direction of the channel
  Carcassi imposes by choosing \(L = a^\dagger\) is the \(+ic\)
  orientation of the expansion (Theorem 19.5.1 of {[}24{]}).
\item
  \textbf{Physics is relations between ensembles of registrations, and
  the Born rule is one-to-one with entropy} (Carcassi 1:19:16--1:21:47)
  give, with the conservation of entropy under unitaries, the statement
  that without measurement there is no quantum mechanics, and locate
  Susskind's unitarity claim {[}82{]} as a theorem of the Algebraic
  Channel that omits the registration (§6.4.4). McGucken's contribution:
  the registration is a physical process of the apparatus at the locus
  \(x_4 = ict\) with rate \(\Gamma_{\text{Wick}} \sim N\omega_C\)
  (Theorem 25 of {[}24{]}), irreversible by \(+ic\).
\item
  \textbf{Every quantum effect from the lower bound on entropy, ``I
  still don't know how''} (Carcassi 1:13:14--1:14:20) is answered item

  (§3.14), entanglement (one Sphere measured at two points, §5.9), the

\item
  \textbf{Classical mechanics as the high-entropy limit, with

  \(dx_4/dt = ic\), and the mechanism Carcassi leaves unspecified is the
