corrections, or a horizon mode density that is not area-proportional,
would refute the horizon reading of Ω.

Third, the identity fails if the event Compton scale and the horizon
temperature do not share the common origin the framework claims. The
identification ties the Hawking temperature (a genuine
Kubo--Martin--Schwinger periodicity: the Euclidean x₄-period at the
horizon, §C.3, Theorem 13) and the Compton energy scale at the event
(\(mc^2/k_B\), the intrinsic \(x_4\)-oscillation frequency, §C.2) to the
one \(x_4\)-advance rate of the McGucken Sphere. The horizon is a bona
fide thermal KMS state; the event carries the Compton \emph{energy
scale} set by the same advance rate, not a horizon-type KMS periodicity
(a single Compton phase does not Wick-rotate to a periodic correlator,
§C.2). If the horizon temperature and the event Compton scale were found
to have no common origin in the \(x_4\)-advance --- for instance if the
Hawking temperature did not track the same advance rate that sets
\(\omega_C\) --- the identification would fail.

Fourth, and distinguishing: the identity predicts that Born-rule
probabilities are modified by spacetime curvature, because the cell
count N is the same count the gravitational field reads on the horizon.
In the standard treatment, where the Born entropy and the gravitational
entropy are different objects, there is no reason for the quantum
probability measure to depend on the local gravitational field beyond
the known effects of gravitational time dilation on frequencies and
phases. In the McGucken \(dx_4/dt = ic\) framework, where the Born
measure and the gravitational entropy are readings of the same count of
distinguishable cells of the McGucken Sphere, the local x₄-advance rate
--- set by the gravitational field through gravitational time dilation
--- enters the count N, and outcomes that sample regions of the Sphere
at different advance rates acquire a relative dependence on the
\emph{difference} in rate beyond the standard phase effect. The form of
the dependence is fixed by the equivalence principle, which the
framework derives (GR T4, §5). A branch at potential \(\Phi_a\) carries
a count rescaled by the time-dilation factor,
\(N_a \to (1 + \Phi_a/c^2)\,N_a\) (for massive branches the count is of
Compton ticks, for photon branches of phase cycles \(\omega/2\pi\) per
coordinate time), so that in the normalized measure
\(p_a = N_a/\sum_b N_b\) a potential common to all branches cancels and
a first-order potential difference gives
\(\delta p_a = p_a\,(\Phi_a - \sum_b p_b \Phi_b)/c^2\). For a
\emph{uniform} field, however, this first-order term must vanish: by the
Einstein equivalence principle a uniform field is an accelerated frame
in flat spacetime, where the Born statistics are frame-independent, and
the count rescaling of the two branches is then a common factor removed
by the normalization once the branches are compared on the common
spatial slice of the Sphere (the uniform-field potential difference is a
difference of clock rates, which changes the phase accumulated along
each branch and leaves the cell count of the joint Sphere invariant).
The leading surviving term is therefore the one the equivalence
principle permits --- the tidal term, second order in the branch
separation \(L\) and first order in the Riemann curvature: the
x₄-advance rates of the two branches differ by the relative acceleration
of neighbouring Spheres,
\(\delta(\dot x_4/c)/(\dot x_4/c) \sim R_{0i0j}L^iL^j\), giving a shift
in the outcome measure
\[\delta p_a \;\sim\; p_a\, R_{0i0j}\,L^i L^j \;\sim\; p_a\,\frac{GM}{c^2 r^3}\,L^2\]
for branches separated by \(L\) at distance \(r\) from a mass \(M\). The
magnitude is \(\sim 2\times10^{-23}\) for \(L = 1\) m at the Earth's
surface and \(\sim 10^{-9}\) for \(L = 1\) m at \(r = 10\) km from a
neutron star of \(r_s = 3\) km; it is largest for branches separated
across a steep curvature gradient near compact masses, and
distinguishable from the standard gravitational phase (the
Colella--Overhauser--Werner phase, first order in \(gL\)) because it
appears in the outcome measure, not only in the phase, and scales as
\(L^2 R\) rather than as \(gL\). A measurement finding the Born
statistics independent of the branch curvature difference to the
precision set by \(R_{0i0j}L^iL^j\), where the framework predicts
dependence, would refute the identification. This is the test that
separates ``gravity is the Born rule'' from the two-entropy picture, in
which no such dependence is predicted; the first-order uniform-field
version, \(\delta p_a \propto \Delta\Phi/c^2\), is excluded by the
equivalence principle in both pictures, and a derivation that produced
it would contradict GR T4.

\hypertarget{scope}{%
\subsection{10. Scope}\label{scope}}

Everything in this paper descends from one physical principle, the
McGucken Principle \(dx_4/dt = ic\): the fourth dimension expanding at
the rate c, as a spherically symmetric wavefront, from every point of
spacetime. The results are theorem chains descending from that common,
foundational, physical principle, in the spirit of Newton and Euclid,
who each derived a wide body of results from a small foundation stated
at the outset. The claim of this paper is precise, and its boundary is
stated here. What is derived independently from \(dx_4/dt = ic\) is each
endpoint. The Born rule is derived in Section 3 as the unique
SO(3)-invariant measure on the McGucken Sphere, with the exponent two
forced by the rank-two metric and unitarity {[}19, 20{]}. Gravity is
derived in Section 4 as the horizon thermodynamics of the McGucken
Sphere, with the Bekenstein--Hawking entropy the count of Planck-scale
McGucken Spheres tiling the horizon {[}25, 31{]}. Both derivations
descend from the McGucken Principle \(dx_4/dt = ic\) and stand on their
own {[}23, 29{]}.

The identity ``gravity is the Born rule'' is the transitive consequence
of both being the same cell count N of distinguishable states of the one
McGucken Sphere --- the gravitational entropy its logarithmic horizon
reading S = k ln Ω = k N/4 and the Born measure its normalized event
reading. The claim is that the two entropy-connections of the
literature, kept separate there because they use two different entropies
in two different spaces, are one connection in the McGucken
\(dx_4/dt = ic\) framework because the framework's entropy is a single
physical count. This is a unification of two established results ---
gravity = entropy {[}1, 2, 3, 4{]} and Born rule = entropy {[}5, 6, 7,
8, 9, 10{]} --- and not an additional postulate: nothing is assumed
beyond \(dx_4/dt = ic\) and the two derivations it yields {[}23, 29{]}.

Two limits are stated plainly. First, the shared-count identity of
Section 7 rests on the physical claim that the McGucken Sphere's
x₄-advance is one process whose state count Ω is read over the
directional cross-section in the Born case and over the causal boundary
in the gravitational case. This is a physical identification of two
readings of one count, supported by the isotropy and one-cycle
resolution of \(dx_4/dt = ic\); it is not a derivation of the horizon
area law from the Born measure or of the Born measure from the area law,
since each is derived independently from \(dx_4/dt = ic\) {[}19, 31{]}
and the identity is their transitive consequence. Second, the
falsifiability of Section 9 is what makes the identity a physical claim;
its fourth prediction --- a curvature (tidal) dependence of the Born
measure of order \(R_{0i0j}L^iL^j\) for branches separated by L,
tracking the horizon count --- is the distinguishing test, and the
identification stands or fails by it.

The result belongs to the general thesis of the McGucken corpus. Gravity
and the Born rule, which the literature relates each to a separate
entropy and never to each other, are one fact about the expanding
McGucken Sphere generated at every event by \(dx_4/dt = ic\): the count
of x₄-states, read over the horizon as gravity and over the event as the
Born rule. They share an entropy because they share a source. Quantum
mechanics, general relativity, thermodynamics, and the symmetries and
conservation laws are theorem-chains of the one Principle {[}18, 22, 28,
29, 30, 35{]}, and the equivalences the literature finds among them ---
gravity with entropy, the Born rule with entropy, the third law with the
uncertainty principle, and now gravity with the Born rule --- exist
because each theory is a reading of the single physical reality that the
McGucken Principle \(dx_4/dt = ic\) names: the fourth dimension
expanding at the rate c, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every
point of spacetime.

\hypertarget{appendix-a.-explicit-computation-of-ux3c9-the-number-of-distinguishable-compton-tick-states-of-the-mcgucken-sphere-counted-on-the-directional-cross-section-giving-the-born-measure-and-on-the-horizon-giving-the-gravitational-entropy-with-the-proof-that-the-two-counts-are-one-so3-invariant-measure}{%
\subsection{Appendix A. Explicit computation of Ω, the number of
distinguishable Compton-tick states of the McGucken Sphere, counted on
the directional cross-section (giving the Born measure) and on the
horizon (giving the gravitational entropy), with the proof that the two
counts are one SO(3)-invariant
measure}\label{appendix-a.-explicit-computation-of-ux3c9-the-number-of-distinguishable-compton-tick-states-of-the-mcgucken-sphere-counted-on-the-directional-cross-section-giving-the-born-measure-and-on-the-horizon-giving-the-gravitational-entropy-with-the-proof-that-the-two-counts-are-one-so3-invariant-measure}}

The McGucken Principle \(dx_4/dt = ic\) generates at every event the
expanding McGucken Sphere, whose distinguishable states are counted by
Ω. This appendix computes Ω explicitly, on the directional cross-section
and on the horizon, and shows the two are one measure.

\textbf{A.1 The cross-section count.} The McGucken Sphere at event p has
cross-section S², the unit 2-sphere of null directions. The x₄-advance
carries action \(h\) per Compton cycle (Section 2), and the transverse
resolution of one cycle is the Compton wavelength \(h/mc\). A region
\(R ⊆ S²\) of solid-angle measure \(Ω_Ω(R) = ∫_R \sinθ\,dθ\,dφ\)
subtends, at radius r = ct on the Sphere, an area \(r²Ω_Ω(R)\), which at
cycle resolution contains

\[N(R) = \frac{r^2\,\Omega_\Omega(R)}{(h/mc)^2}\]

resolution cells. The distinguishable states of the Sphere over R number
N(R), and the SO(3)-invariant probability weight of \(R\) is

\[\int_R d\mu = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_R \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi = \frac{\Omega_\Omega(R)}{4\pi}.\]

The invariance of dμ under SO(3) is verified directly: under a rotation
\(g ∈ SO(3)\), \(\sinθ\, dθ\, dφ\) is the pullback of the round area
form, which is rotation-invariant, so \(∫_{gR} dμ = ∫_R dμ\). Uniqueness
follows because any two SO(3)-invariant probability measures on the
homogeneous space S² = SO(3)/SO(2) coincide with the normalized Haar
measure by the Riesz representation theorem: an invariant positive
normalized functional on C(S²) is unique.

\textbf{A.2 The Born probability from the count.} For an outcome
direction φ = \textbar0⟩ (the north pole, unit vector \(\hat{n}\)\_φ)
and a state ψ whose Bloch direction \(\hat{n}\)\_ψ makes polar angle θ
with \(\hat{n}\)\_φ (the Fubini--Study identification of the state with
a direction on the Sphere's cross-section, Appendix B), the outcome
region is the zone of the cross-section lying on the detector side of
the plane perpendicular to \(\hat{n}\)\_φ through the projection of the
state's antipode,
\[R_\varphi = \{\hat{n} \in S^2 : \hat{n}\cdot\hat{n}_\varphi \ge -\,\hat{n}_\psi\cdot\hat{n}_\varphi = -\cos\theta\}.\]
By Archimedes' hat-box theorem the SO(3)-invariant measure of a zone is
proportional to its height, so
\[\int_{R_\varphi} d\mu = \frac{1 - (-\cos\theta)}{2} = \frac{1+\cos\theta}{2} = \cos^2(\theta/2),\]
the Malus projection of Proposition 7.5: the transmitted fraction is the
height of the zone cut by the state's projection on the detector axis.
The selection rule is therefore fixed by the two directions the
measurement involves, \(\hat{n}\)\_ψ (the state) and \(\hat{n}\)\_φ (the
detector axis), and by nothing else; an arbitrary cap of the same
measure is not the construction. What the construction takes as input is
the representation of the state by a direction on the Sphere, which is
Appendix B's identification of the Sphere's cross-section with the
projective state space. Hence

\[p(\varphi\mid\psi) = \frac{N(R_\varphi)}{N(S^2)} = \frac{\int_{R_\varphi}d\mu}{\int_{S^2}d\mu} = \cos^2(\theta/2) = |\langle 0\mid\psi\rangle|^2,\]

the resolution scale λ\_C and radius r cancelling between numerator and
denominator. N(R) is the cell count; the Born rule is its normalized
value.

\textbf{A.3 The horizon count.} Let H be the local Rindler horizon
through p --- the patch of the null cone of Σ₊(p) on which Theorem 14
reads the Clausius relation --- with area A(H). Tiling H by Planck-scale
McGucken Spheres, one per Planck area ℓ\_P² = ℏG/c³, gives

\[N(H) = \frac{A(H)}{\ell_P^2}\]

boundary cells. Each cell carries one Compton-tick boundary mode and one
quarter of a nat of entropy, the factor of one quarter fixed in the
Geometric Channel by Newtonian matching of the Clausius relation to the
Einstein field equations (Theorem 14 with Theorem 9 Step 6, the same
matching Jacobson uses) and confirmed from the Algebraic-Channel action
by the Euclidean cigar (Theorem 12, Step C); the microstate count and
the entropy are

\[\Omega(H) = e^{N(H)/4} = \exp\!\left(\frac{A(H)}{4\ell_P^2}\right), \qquad S_H = k_B\ln\Omega(H) = \frac{k_B N(H)}{4} = \frac{k_B A(H)}{4\ell_P^2}.\]

The cell count N(H) is the surface measure; Ω(H) is its exponential. The
Born reading of §A.2 uses N as a ratio; the gravitational reading uses N
through ln Ω = N/4.

\textbf{A.3bis Area-scaling, not volume-scaling: which count is which.}
A clarification prevents a common conflation. The two readings that give
the identity of §7 --- the gravitational entropy and the Born measure
--- are counts of Ω over a \emph{bounding surface}, not over an enclosed
volume: the gravitational cell count N(H) is tiled over the horizon
\emph{area} A(H), one Compton-tick mode per Planck area (giving the
holographic area law S = k\_B ln Ω = k\_B N(H)/4 = k\_B A/4ℓ\_P², §A.3),
and the Born count is taken over the \emph{directional cross-section}
--- the S² of directions of the Sphere at the event, the SO(3)-invariant
angular measure (§A.1, §3.2). Both are surface counts, and their
area-scaling is the holographic content: the entropy of a region scales
with its boundary, not its bulk. This is distinct from the separate
statement, used in the Second Law (§4.1, §3.11), that the Sphere's
expansion \emph{augments phase-space volume} and thereby increases
entropy by the Boltzmann relation S = k\_B ln W with W the phase-space
volume {[}40{]}. The phase-space-volume growth is the thermodynamic
driver of the arrow of time; the spatial entropy of gravity and the Born
measure scale with surface area by holography. The two should not be
conflated: Ω grows as the Sphere expands, but the gravitational and Born
readings count Ω over the bounding surface, while the Second-Law reading
counts the growth of phase-space volume.

\textbf{A.4 One measure, two surfaces.} The cross-section count (A.1)
and the horizon count (A.3) are the same SO(3)-invariant cell measure N
of the advance-state space, integrated over two surfaces of the one null
cone. On S² the measure is dμ per resolution cell; on H the cell density
is 1/ℓ\_P² per unit area, uniform over H because SO(3)-invariance of
\(dx_4/dt = ic\) forbids a direction-dependent density. Both are the
invariant advance-state measure restricted to a surface. The Born rule
integrates N over the directional cross-section and normalizes; gravity
integrates N over the local horizon and reads it through the logarithm
of Ω = e\^{}\{N/4\}. This is what Theorem 7.3 establishes.

\hypertarget{appendix-b.-the-fubinistudy-fisherrao-identity-on-the-mcgucken-sphere}{%
\subsection{Appendix B. The Fubini--Study = Fisher--Rao identity on the
McGucken
Sphere}\label{appendix-b.-the-fubinistudy-fisherrao-identity-on-the-mcgucken-sphere}}

The McGucken Principle \(dx_4/dt = ic\) generates the expanding McGucken
Sphere whose directional cross-section carries the quantum state. This
appendix shows that the metric geometry of that cross-section and its
statistical distinguishability geometry are one geometry, with the Born
rule the map between them --- the Geometric-Channel derivation of the
Born rule referenced in Section 8.

\textbf{B.1 The Fubini--Study metric.} On the projective space of states
--- the McGucken Sphere's cross-section, CP¹ = S² for a two-state system
--- the Fubini--Study line element between neighbouring states
\textbar ψ⟩ and \textbar ψ + dψ⟩ is

\[ds_{\text{FS}}^2 = \langle d\psi\mid d\psi\rangle - |\langle\psi\mid d\psi\rangle|^2.\]

For \textbar ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)\textbar0⟩ + e\^{}\{iφ\}sin(θ/2)\textbar1⟩
this evaluates to

\[ds_{\text{FS}}^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right),\]

one quarter of the round metric on S² --- the intrinsic metric geometry
of the McGucken Sphere's directions.

\textbf{B.2 The Fisher--Rao metric.} The statistical distinguishability
of two probability distributions \{p\_i\} and \{p\_i + dp\_i\} is
measured by the Fisher--Rao line element

\[ds_{\text{FR}}^2 = \frac{1}{4}\sum_i \frac{dp_i^2}{p_i}.\]

For the Born distribution \(p_i = |\langle i|\psi\rangle|^2\) over
outcomes of a single fixed measurement the Fisher--Rao metric sees only
the component of the displacement that measurement resolves: for the
z-basis, with p\_0 = cos²(θ/2), p\_1 = sin²(θ/2), it is
\(\tfrac14 d\theta^2\) and carries no φ-dependence, while a measurement
in the equatorial plane resolves \(\tfrac14\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\). The
metric that equals the Fubini--Study metric is the maximum of the
Fisher--Rao metric over all measurements (all POVMs) at the point ---
the quantum Fisher information metric of Braunstein and Caves {[}80{]},
who prove that this maximum is attained and equals the Fubini--Study
metric (in the normalization used here):

\[ds_{\text{FR}}^2 \;:=\; \max_{\text{measurements}} \tfrac14\sum_i \frac{dp_i^2}{p_i} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4}\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right).\]

The statistical distance of Wootters {[}9{]} is this optimized
distinguishability; it is the quantity the identity below refers to, and
a single fixed measurement gives its restriction to one direction.

\textbf{B.3 The identity and the Born rule.} Comparing B.1 and B.2,

\[ds_{\text{FS}}^2 = ds_{\text{FR}}^2,\]

the Fubini--Study metric equals the (measurement-optimized) Fisher--Rao
metric on the McGucken Sphere (Wootters {[}9{]}, Braunstein--Caves
{[}80{]}). The map that makes them coincide is the Born rule: it is the
unique assignment p\_i = \textbar⟨i\textbar ψ⟩\textbar² of probabilities
to amplitudes under which the metric distance between states equals
their statistical distinguishability. Any exponent p ≠ 2 breaks the
equality --- \textbar⟨i\textbar ψ⟩\textbar\^{}p gives a Fisher--Rao
metric proportional to a p-dependent factor that matches the
Fubini--Study metric only at p = 2. The Born exponent is the exponent
that identifies the McGucken Sphere's metric geometry with its
distinguishability geometry, which is the Geometric-Channel statement of
the Haar-route derivation of Section 3.

\hypertarget{appendix-c.-the-kms-structure-compton-and-hawking-temperatures-as-one-periodicity}{%
\subsection{Appendix C. The KMS structure: Compton and Hawking
temperatures as one
periodicity}\label{appendix-c.-the-kms-structure-compton-and-hawking-temperatures-as-one-periodicity}}

The McGucken Principle \(dx_4/dt = ic\) generates the expanding McGucken
Sphere, which oscillates at the Compton rate at the event and,
Wick-rotated, is periodic in Euclidean x₄. This appendix shows that the
Compton temperature of the Sphere at the event and the Hawking
temperature at the horizon are two readings of one
Kubo--Martin--Schwinger periodicity, the shared-temperature structure
underlying the third falsifiability test of Section 9.

\textbf{C.1 The KMS condition.} A thermal state at inverse temperature β
is characterized by the Kubo--Martin--Schwinger condition: the two-point
function G(t) of the state is periodic in imaginary time with period βℏ,

\[G(t - i\beta\hbar) = G(t).\]

Under the McGucken--Wick rotation t → −iτ, the Lorentzian x₄ = ict
becomes the Euclidean x₄ = cτ, and a KMS state is a state periodic in
the Euclidean x₄-direction with period βℏc.

\textbf{C.2 The Compton energy scale at the event.} The McGucken Sphere
oscillates with Compton period \(T_C = h/mc^2\) (Section 2), setting an
intrinsic frequency \(\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar\) and a characteristic
energy \(\hbar\omega_C = mc^2\). By \(E = k_B T\), this fixes a
characteristic temperature scale
\[T_C^{\text{temp}} \;=\; \frac{mc^2}{k_B}\] at the event. This is a
dimensional energy-scale identification, not a claim that the event is a
thermal KMS state: a single Compton phase \(e^{-imc^2 t/\hbar}\) does
not Wick-rotate to a periodic Euclidean correlator (under
\(t\to -i\tau\) it becomes the real exponential
\(e^{-mc^2\tau/\hbar}\)), so the event carries the Compton \emph{energy
scale} \(mc^2\) but not a horizon-type KMS periodicity. The genuine KMS
thermal structure of the framework is the horizon periodicity of §C.3
(and Theorem 13), which does arise from a bona fide Euclidean
periodicity; the event Compton scale and the horizon temperature are
related by the shared \(x_4\)-advance rate, not by an identity of KMS
states.

\textbf{C.3 The Hawking temperature at the horizon.} Near a horizon of
surface gravity κ, regularity of the Euclidean section under t → −iτ
requires the Euclidean x₄-axis to close with period 2πc/κ, giving the
KMS inverse temperature β\_H = 2π/κℏ and

\[T_H = \frac{\hbar\kappa}{2\pi k_B c} = \frac{\hbar c^3}{8\pi G M k_B}\]

for a black hole of mass M (κ = c⁴/4GM). The McGucken Sphere at the
horizon is a KMS state at the Hawking temperature.

\textbf{C.4 One advance rate.} Both scales descend from the one
\(x_4\)-advance rate of the same McGucken Sphere under the
McGucken--Wick rotation --- the Compton energy scale \(mc^2/k_B\) read
at the event (the intrinsic oscillation frequency, §C.2), and the
genuine Hawking KMS temperature read at the horizon (the Euclidean
x₄-period, §C.3). The horizon reading is a bona fide thermal KMS state;
the event reading is the energy scale set by the same advance rate. They
are two readings of the one \(dx_4/dt = ic\) advance, not a single KMS
state shared between event and horizon. The identity ``gravity is the
Born rule'' requires only the weaker, correct statement: the Born
measure (event reading) and the gravitational entropy (horizon reading)
descend from the one Sphere generated by the one advance rate.

\hypertarget{appendix-d.-the-arakiuhlmann-relative-entropy-as-a-theorem-of-the-mcgucken-principle-dxux2084dt-ic}{%
\subsection{Appendix D. The Araki--Uhlmann relative entropy as a theorem
of the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt =
ic}\label{appendix-d.-the-arakiuhlmann-relative-entropy-as-a-theorem-of-the-mcgucken-principle-dxux2084dt-ic}}

\textbf{McGucken Principle anchor.} The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic
states the physical reality that the fourth dimension expands at the
rate c, as a spherically symmetric wavefront --- the McGucken Sphere,
whose wavelength carries one quantum of action h per Compton cycle ---
from every event of spacetime. The Araki--Uhlmann relative entropy that
Dorau and Much {[}65{]} use to derive the semiclassical Einstein
equations (§5.12) is, in this framework, a reading of the count Ω of
distinguishable Compton-tick states of that expanding Sphere. This
appendix derives, as theorems of dx₄/dt = ic, the three facts on which
that use rests: the wedge algebra of the McGucken field is a type III₁
factor, so the relative entropy --- rather than the von Neumann entropy
--- is the available measure; its Tomita--Takesaki modular flow is the
x₄-advance read in the uniformly accelerated frame; and the
relative-entropy functional is the count Ω. The standard
operator-algebra theorems (Tomita--Takesaki, Reeh--Schlieder {[}69{]},
Bisognano--Wichmann {[}68{]}, Connes' classification, the Araki--Uhlmann
definition {[}66, 67{]}) are invoked with their hypotheses supplied as
theorems of dx₄/dt = ic --- the same standing as the invocation of
Haar's theorem in §3.2. This appendix is the gravity-side reading of the
corpus derivation given in full in the thermodynamics paper {[}24{]},
§§22.3.9--22.3.10 and Corollaries 22.3.A--22.3.B, where the
Araki--Uhlmann relative entropy, its Uhlmann monotonicity, the Casini
Bekenstein bound, and the Faulkner--Guica--Hartman--Myers--Van Raamsdonk
linearized Einstein equations are each established as theorems of dx₄/dt
= ic on the Sphere-cogenerated wedge algebra; that treatment is
reproduced verbatim in §D.10 below.

\textbf{Theorem D.1 (Araki--Uhlmann relative entropy as a theorem of
dx₄/dt = ic).} \emph{Let dx₄/dt = ic generate at an event p the
expanding McGucken Sphere and its Minkowski space 𝕄₁,₃ (Lemma 2.5). Let
W be the Rindler wedge of a uniformly accelerated observer --- the
region swept by the boost that tilts the +ic axis --- and let 𝒩 be the
von Neumann algebra of the McGucken field on W, with vacuum vector Ω₀.
Then (i) 𝒩 is a hyperfinite type III₁ factor; (ii) its Tomita--Takesaki
modular flow Δ\^{}\{it\} is the boost, the x₄-advance of dx₄/dt = ic
read in the accelerated frame, with modular Hamiltonian K = 2π ∫ U
⟨:T\_UU:⟩ dU on the horizon; (iii) for a coherent excitation ω\_φ the
Araki--Uhlmann relative entropy is S(ω₀‖ω\_φ) = −2π ∫\emph{ℋ U
⟨:T\_ab:⟩}\{ω\_φ\} ξ\^{}a ξ\^{}b dU dvol, the count Ω of Compton-tick
states by which ω\_φ is distinguished from the vacuum on the one
Sphere.}

\textbf{Lemma D.2 (the arena is supplied by dx₄/dt = ic).} From the
Principle: the Minkowski metric η = diag(−c², 1, 1, 1) by the pullback
(ic)² = −c² (Lemma 2.5); the boost Killing field ξ as the frame-rotation
of the +ic axis, null on the two horizon sheets meeting at the
bifurcation surface 𝒮; the real scalar McGucken field Φ with (\ensuremath{\square} + m²)Φ =
0, the massive Huygens extension of the Sphere's wave equation (QM T8 of
{[}38{]}), quantized to the Weyl algebra; and the vacuum Ω₀ as the
overlap of the Spheres expanding at +ic from neighboring events, with
positive energy --- the +ic orientation is the forward advance, so the
x₄-translation generator has non-negative spectrum (the spectrum
condition, {[}29{]} §16.15). Each is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic rather
than a background posit.

\textbf{Lemma D.3 (Ω₀ cyclic and separating --- Reeh--Schlieder,
hypotheses supplied).} Reeh--Schlieder {[}69{]} gives cyclicity and
separation of Ω₀ for 𝒩 from locality, weak additivity, a unique
Poincaré-invariant vacuum, and the spectrum condition. Locality holds
because the Sphere expands at finite c, so operators spacelike to W
commute, the null cone bounding causal contact being the Sphere's own
wavefront; uniqueness and Poincaré invariance of Ω₀ hold by the Sphere's
isotropy and Lorentz invariance (GR T8 of {[}23{]}); the spectrum
condition holds by the +ic positivity of Lemma D.2. The
McGucken-framework form of this cyclicity is {[}29{]} §16.15.8, where it
follows from the per-event universality of dx₄/dt = ic: every event in a
region carries its own +ic Sphere whose wavefront reaches throughout the
causal future, so local operators on the vacuum reach a dense set.
Cyclic-and-separating is the precondition Tomita--Takesaki requires.

\textbf{Lemma D.4 (modular flow = x₄-advance in the accelerated frame).}
Tomita--Takesaki assigns (𝒩, Ω₀) a modular operator Δ and conjugation J
from the polar decomposition of the closure of S₀ : aΩ₀ ↦ a*Ω₀.
Bisognano--Wichmann {[}68{]} evaluate them for the wedge: Δ\^{}\{it\} =
U(Λ\_ξ(−2πt)) is the boost, and J is the TCP--wedge reflection. Under
the McGucken--Wick rotation t → −iτ, τ = x₄/c (§7.4), the boost is the
generator of Euclidean rotation in the (x¹, x₄) plane, and its orbit is
the arc the +ic axis sweeps as the frame accelerates ({[}29{]} §12.8,
Proposition 12.8); so Δ\^{}\{it\} advances the x₄-phase at the wedge,
and the modular flow is the x₄-advance of dx₄/dt = ic read in the
accelerated frame ({[}29{]} §16.14, where the modular flow is the
Lorentz boost). The modular Hamiltonian K = −ln Δ is 2π times the boost
generator ∫\_W x¹ T\^{}\{00\} d³x, which on the horizon is the null form
K = 2π ∫ U ⟨:T\_UU:⟩ dU (Casini--Grillo--Pontello {[}70{]}, Eqs. 1.5,
1.9). Bisognano--Wichmann supplies the second modular object as well:
the modular conjugation J = Θ·R₁(π), acting on the field as J Φ(x⁰, x¹,
x², x³) J⁻¹ = Φ*(−x⁰, −x¹, x², x³), a reflection in the (x⁰, x¹) plane
composed with Hermitian conjugation. Under x₄ = ict the x⁰-reflection is
the x₄ → −x₄ reflection that would swap the forward Sphere Σ₊(p) and the
backward Sphere Σ₋(p); the +ic orientation excludes Σ₋(p), so J is the
single-Sphere PT (parity--time) reflection through the source event p
({[}24{]} §22.3.9 (iv)--(v)). This J is the modular partner of the
Born-rule PT-symmetry route (Theorem 7.11, §3.9): the same reflection
through the source event that carries complex conjugation ψ ↦ ψ* in the
Born density appears here as the modular conjugation of the wedge
algebra.

\textbf{Lemma D.5 (KMS periodicity --- the Euclidean x₄-period).} The
vacuum restricted to 𝒩 is a KMS state at inverse temperature β = 2π/κ
with respect to the modular/boost flow. This is Appendix C.3 (Theorem
13): regularity of the Euclidean section under t → −iτ forces the
Euclidean x₄-axis to close with period 2πc/κ, giving β\_H = 2π/κℏ and
the Unruh/Hawking temperature T = ℏκ/2πk\_Bc. By Tomita--Takesaki the
KMS property at β = 2π/κ is equivalent to the modular identification of
Lemma D.4; the Euclidean x₄-period of the Sphere supplies it.

\textbf{Lemma D.6 (type III₁, which forces relative entropy in place of
von Neumann entropy).} Connes' S-invariant is S(𝒩) = ∩\_φ spec(Δ\_φ)
over all faithful normal states φ. The modular operator of Lemma D.4 is
Δ\_Ω = e\^{}\{−2π·(boost generator)\}; the Lorentz boost generator has
spectrum all of ℝ, continuous and unbounded in both directions, so
spec(Δ\_Ω) = (0,∞) with no eigenvalue. One state's spectrum bounds the
intersection from above and does not fix it; the classification uses the
Fredenhagen argument reproduced in §D.10 (Theorem 22.3.9 (i) of
{[}24{]}: Fredenhagen 1985, Buchholz--D'Antoni--Fredenhagen 1987), which
shows from asymptotic scale invariance that the modular spectra of all
local algebras are the full (0,∞) for every faithful normal state, so
S(𝒩) = {[}0,∞). By Connes' classification a factor with S = {[}0,∞) is
type III₁; the factor property is Haag duality for the wedge, standard
for the McGucken free field. The full-ℝ spectrum of the x₄-advance
generator read as the boost is the vacuum instance of that result. A
type III₁ factor carries no trace and no density matrix, so the von
Neumann entropy −Tr(ρ ln ρ) is undefined on 𝒩 and the relative entropy
is the available measure --- Dorau--Much's footnote on the type III
structure {[}65{]}, here derived.

\textbf{Lemma D.7 (the relative modular operator and the Araki--Uhlmann
functional).} For the coherent excitation Ω\_φ = W(φ)Ω₀ =
e\^{}\{iΦ(φ)\}Ω₀, the relative modular operator Δ\_\{Ω₀\textbar Ω\_φ\}
is the polar part of the closure of S\_\{Ω₀\textbar Ω\_φ\} : aΩ\_φ ↦
a*Ω₀, and the Araki--Uhlmann relative entropy {[}66, 67{]} is

\[S(\omega_0\Vert\omega_\varphi) = -\langle \Omega_\varphi \,|\, \ln\Delta_{\Omega_0|\Omega_\varphi}\,|\,\Omega_\varphi\rangle,\]

representative-independent (Araki {[}66{]}, Eq. 1.1) and reducing in the
finite-dimensional case to Tr(ρ\_φ ln ρ\_φ) − Tr(ρ\_φ ln ρ₀) (Eq. 1.2).
For any normal state the functional decomposes exactly as S = Δ⟨K⟩ − ΔS,
the change in the modular-Hamiltonian expectation minus the change in
entanglement entropy (Casini {[}70{]}, Eqs. 17--19;
Casini--Grillo--Pontello {[}70{]}, Eq. 1.6), with positivity S ≥ 0
giving the first-law inequality Δ⟨K⟩ ≥ ΔS (the Bekenstein bound, Casini
{[}70{]}; the first law of entanglement,
Faulkner--Guica--Hartman--Myers--Van Raamsdonk {[}70{]}, δS = δ⟨K⟩). For
a coherent state the Weyl displacement W(φ) is unitary, so the
entanglement change vanishes, ΔS = 0 (Casini--Grillo--Pontello
{[}70{]}), and

\[S(\omega_0\Vert\omega_\varphi) = \langle \Omega_\varphi \,|\, K \,|\, \Omega_\varphi\rangle = -2\pi\!\int_\mathcal{H} U\,\langle :T_{ab}: \rangle_{\omega_\varphi}\,\xi^a\xi^b\,dU\,d\mathrm{vol} = 2\pi\!\int_{x^1>0} x^1\,\langle \Phi, T_{00}\,\Phi\rangle\,,\]

positive since U \textless{} 0 on the right horizon portion
(Casini--Grillo--Pontello {[}70{]}, Eq. 1.18; Kurpicz--Pinamonti--Verch
on the trapping horizon; Dorau--Much {[}65{]}, Eqs. 12--13). The
functional rests on a modular operator that is the x₄-advance (Lemma
D.4) of an algebra that is type III₁ (Lemma D.6), both theorems of the
Principle.

\textbf{Lemma D.8 (the functional is the +ic count Ω).} On the horizon
⟨:T\_UU:⟩ is the energy flux --- the rate at which the Compton-tick
action h of the excited Sphere crosses per unit affine coordinate U. The
modular integral −2π ∫ U ⟨:T\_UU:⟩ dU weights those Compton-tick quanta
by the affine horizon coordinate, counting the distinguishable +ic
Compton-tick states by which the excited Sphere ω\_φ differs from the
vacuum Sphere ω₀. That count is Ω, so for the coherent excitation above
the vacuum S(ω₀‖ω\_φ) = k\_B ln(Ω\_φ/Ω₀) with Ω\_φ ≥ Ω₀ --- the
excitation adds Compton-tick quanta, which is the positivity of the
horizon-flux integral (U \textless{} 0 on the right horizon portion,
Lemma D.7) --- the McGucken Entropy S = k ln Ω (§6) read on the horizon
as the distinguishability of the excited state from the vacuum. The
count-ratio form is this one-sided statement for excitations above the
vacuum; the general Araki--Uhlmann functional is the two-state modular
quantity of Lemma D.7, non-negative in both orderings, and the ratio of
two independently assigned counts does not represent it in general (the
swapped ordering would reverse the sign). By Theorem 7.3 this horizon
count is the same Ω the Bekenstein--Hawking area law reads, so the
Araki--Uhlmann relative entropy and the gravitational entropy are one
count of one Sphere --- the identity ``gravity is the Born rule'' (§7)
standing at the type III₁ modular level at which Dorau--Much {[}65{]}
work. ∎

\textbf{D.9 Scope.} The general decomposition S = Δ⟨K⟩ − ΔS is a
count-difference of Compton-tick states for every state of the field:
the horizon-flux count and the cross-horizon entanglement count, both of
the one expanding McGucken Sphere. The clean reduction S = Δ⟨K⟩ holds
for coherent and Weyl-reachable states, where ΔS = 0. For general
(non-coherent) states the functional is constrained by the Uhlmann
monotonicity (data-processing inequality) S(φ∘α‖ψ∘α) ≤ S(φ‖ψ), which
{[}24{]} §22.3.10 derives from the SO(3)-Haar-measure contraction of the
Sphere under coarse-graining (Stinespring dilation, Lieb concavity, Petz
sufficiency for the equality case); so the general-state direction is
governed, not open. What remains without a closed form is the explicit
relative modular operator of an arbitrary non-coherent state, which has
no general closed expression --- an open computation shared with the
whole algebraic quantum field theory program, not peculiar to dx₄/dt =
ic. The local-Minkowski step of Dorau--Much (their Eq. 1) is, in this
framework, the exact metric of Lemma 2.5, with the shear and vorticity
of the horizon-generating congruence vanishing exactly by the Sphere's
isotropy (§4.1) rather than approximately on a Killing horizon, and the
curvature correction the tidal rescaling of the local Compton-tick rate
between neighbouring Spheres, of order R\_\{0i0j\}L\textsuperscript{iL}j
(§9); the all-orders modular data on a curved horizon is the same future
computation Dorau--Much flag {[}65{]}. The three results of Theorem D.1
--- type III₁, the modular flow as the x₄-advance, and the functional as
the count Ω --- rest on the operator-algebra theorems {[}66, 67, 68,
69{]} with their hypotheses supplied by dx₄/dt = ic (Lemmas D.2--D.6)
and on the first-law and coherent-state results {[}70{]}, with the
McGucken-side inputs --- the exact metric (Lemma 2.5), the
cyclic-separating vacuum ({[}29{]} §16.15.8), and the boost = x₄-advance
reading ({[}29{]} §12.8, §16.14) --- theorems of the Principle.
